LEWIS (West Huron) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 71) respecting assaults and offences against the person. He said:	The purpose of this Bill
is explained by its title. I have added to it the provision of the Bill which I introduced last year relating to homicide by hunters in the woods. I cannot explain this clause more clearly than by using the words of an editorial in the Ottawa * Citizen ' :
Hunting is a sport. Homicide is a crime. When a keen or careless sportsman in the bush sees something that he thinks is a deer, he fires at it, and subsequently discovers that he has killed a man. If he had seen his target properly he would have known beyond doubt whether it was a deer or a man. Not seeing it properly, he is not sure which it is, but he deliberately takes the chance of killing a man rather than miss shooting a deer. In other words, he does not give the human being the benefit of the doubt. If he gave the deer the benefit of the doubt, and it got away, he would lose about ten dollars' worth of venison. If he gave the man the benefit of the doubt, the life of a human being would be saved. Any hunter who will run the risk of killing a human being rather than risk losing ten dollars' worth of venison deserves to be in the penitentiary. Therefore, the ' Citizen ' thinks that the Bill of Mr. Lewis, M.P., to amend the Criminal Code should pass.
The other clauses of the Bill refer to assaults upon women and to punishment of tramps. I have here small items from newspapers from many parts of Canada. I may just mention some of them:	A despatch from Barrie, * Young farmer committed on charge of criminal assault '; from Stratford, * Stratford girl attacked; Cries frightened the man and he fled;' from London, ' Frightened to death by a tramp;' from Winnipeg, 'Another brute;' from Winnipeg, 'Tinsmith arrested; charged with criminal assault upon a child;' from Vancouver, ' Fiendish murder of a

seven-year-old.' This Bill proposes heavier punishment for such offences. How often, when a man is arrested for stealing-even if he has only stolen something to eat- the offender gets from three to five or even ten years. I have before me a newspaper item about a man getting fifteen years for breaking into a car in the city of Victoria. Here is another about a man who got three years for sending indecent post cards. But the man who assaults a child of five years gets only three months. This Bill propos_es to punish the wrong doer in such cases in such a way as to prevent the recurrence of such crimes.
Another clause has to do with what may be called a custom in this country which leads more to crimes by tramps than any other. In Ontario, at least, it is quite common for a magistrate before whom a prisoner is brought for having no visible means of support, to allow the man to go on the condition that he moves to another county. And in how many cases is that productive of crime? Take the case of the horrible murder committed in the city of Stratford, for which the criminal has just paid the last penalty; within the three weeks before that crime was committed that man had been arrested four times and had been allowed to go on condition of going into another county. The Bill empowers the magistrate, in the ease of a man arrested the second time as a vagrant, to send him into confinement under indeterminate sentence as a dangerous character to be at large.
And, Mr. Speaker, in view of the information contained in the newspapers to some items of which I have already referred, and many others which I have collected, I would ask your permission to say to the government that, in my opinion this Bill and others relating to criminal law should be referred to a committee for consideration. It is twenty years since the Criminal Code was really revised. I would suggest that the Committee on Privileges and Elections, which is a large committee with little to do, a committee composed of lawyers, experts in the enforcement of the criminal law, should have its power enlarged so that it may take into consideration this question of our Criminal Code and the amendments proposed thereto. In accordance with this purpose, it might be called the Committee on Privileges, Elections and the Criminal Law.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. LEWIS moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 72) respecting the saving of daylight. He said : This is the Bill which I introduced last year, and which was considered and favourably reported by a committee of this House. I wish to say that of all the replies we have received, from one end of the country to the other, by boards of trade and by councils, we have had only one objection advanced against the provision of this Bill. When the Bill was first brought up in the imperial House it was laughed at; but it was brought up again, and on the second occasion the House saw fit to appoint a committee of nine members to examine the Bill, and that committee reported absolutely in its favour It has come before the imperial House again, and the imperial House has found one or two reasons, on the eve of an election, why it would not be suitable for England. But those reasons do not apply to this country, and in England they are only thought to apply to the city of London and other large cities, in so far as it might affect theatres and the milk trade. Now, Sir, I contend that if this Bill were passed by this House it would operate one of the most beneficent revolutions in Canada, and after the people had tried it three months it would be absolutely impossible to repeal it. Millions of dollars would be saved to the people now expended on artificial light, and the benefit to public health would be incalculable. The heads of the great railways of this country, the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk, are of the opinion that this Bill would be an incalculable benefit to them; because, if you take the records of the railways themselves, you will find that many, many thousands of dollars loss and many fatal accidents occur which would not occur if the trains were run to a larger extent by daylight, and they would be able to finish their journeys almost entirely by daylight. Now, Sir, I ask the government to appoint a committee to examine this Bill, and I think I may venture to say that there is not an bon. gentleman within the sound of my voice, who has examined and clearly understands this Bill, who is not entirely in favour of it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

That in view of the encouraging results which have come from the money already spent in disseminating information regarding tuberculosis and of the interest which the people of Canada are taking in this question, and also in view of the great saving in life which has been brought about in other countries by practical work in this connection, this House is of the opinion that parliament should now take more active steps to further lessen the great suffering and mortality caused by this disease.

He said: My reason for bringing up this question separately from that of general public health, the subject of a resolution introduced in the House last session, is that the disease to which my resolution refers causes more deaths in this Dominion than all of the directly contagious diseases, and also that it is one which it is peculiarly proper that this government and parliament should deal with, inasmuch as it is widespread throughout all the provinces of the Dominion and can only be properly dealt with the Dominion authority. I would therefore ask the kind consideration of all members of this House to this question, and particularly of those who are doctors in medicine, for as a layman I feel considerable difficulty in speaking on this subject. My reason for speaking is that I feel that this is one of the great questions of our day and generation and one in which we can accomplish a great deal of good.
I do not propose to enter into details or any lengthy explanation concerning the nature of this disease. It is too well known amongst us, particularly in its commoner form of consumption of the lungs. We all know that some years ago it was supposed to be hereditary, and also to be practically incurable. We now know that it is not in-h.erited; we also know that many cases, in fact I may say the greater proportion of cases, can be cured if taken at the proper time. We also know that the children of consumptives have not necessarily to have this disease, since it is not inherited, but it may be contracted afterwards. This disease is caused by a living germ, one that is directly contagious and easily communicated. At the same time, fortunately for us, the disease may be prevented by destroying the sputum of the patient. But the gieat danger at present is from the ignorance of the patient who is at home or on the streets. To-day the great object is to get at the source of the contagion. To slimy that it is easy to prevent this contagion, we have only to call attention to the fact that it is now stated that the place in which any one is least likely to contract consumption is in a properly organized sanatorium. This disease of tuberculosis is curable to a large extent if taken in time, and there have been many efforts made in this direction of late years. In some countries they have established sanatoria, but in Canada this is properly a subject for the provincial governments to take up. In other countries they use to a large extent the open air treatment in inexpensive shacks, where the cost is not very large, and where very good results have been obtained. We are making progress along those lines in many directions, and we are learning by experience. But although much has been done to relieve suffering and to prevent the spread of this dread destroyer of humanity, and although 44*
I am glad to see that a large number of people are taking an interest in this question, at the same time the fight is really only just begun. Dr. Woods Hutchinson,) who is a well known writer on bacteriology, has made the following declaration before the Tuberculosis Exhibition held in New York last fall:
Tuberculosis can be stamped out in New York city within ten years. Ten thousand lives a year can be saved from its ravages. A winning fight can be started within a year.
This is the opinion of an expert, and if this can be done in New York city, how much more easily it can be done in this Canada of ours, where fortunately at the present time we have no such large cities as New' York.'Conditions here are such that it is very much easier for us to fight the disease than it is in an overgrown city. During the last few years, more and more interest has been taken in the question of fighting this dread disease of tuberculosis, and the great work has been carried on in almost every country in the world. In 1906 an international congress was held at the Hague at which sixteen countries were represented. Last year an international congress was held at Washington in the United States, at which was represented almost every country in the world. An official report of that congress has been made, but it covers many volumes, and I do not propose to quote from it here. There is, however, a magazine published in New York called the ' Charities,5 and on its front page it is called a ' Weekly journal of philanthrophy- and social advance.' I would _ like to quote extracts from that magazine to show the nature of the work that was done in Washington last fall, and the good results that have flowed from it. On page 185 of this magazine we read:
From the opening felicitations of Argentina and Austria Monday morning, to the reluctant farewells of Switzerland and Uruguay on Saturday the Tuberculosis Congress showed an intensity and diversity of interest that it would have been difficult to anticipate.
Official delegations from thirty-three nations: a registration of over six thousand members: an attendance sufficient to throng the corridors of the Congress building, pack the section meetings, and tax the hotels of Washington: an exhibit by 438 contributors; and a million and a half sheets of abstracts of papers, printed in Spanish, German, French and English- are a few suggestive statistical items.
On page 204:
Of much more practical and popular interest, for instance, was the exhibit of the work being done in Ireland, by the Women's National Health Association, under the direction of the Countess of Aberdeen. Here was shown how, in the incredibly short period of fourteen months, a whole nation had been aroused to the importance of the problem of eradicating tuberculosis, and by means of a campaign of popular education, on the ' Ameri-

can ' plan, tremendous strides were being made against the disease.
The keynote of all the American exhibits was ' prevention ' rather than statistics or cure. They emphasized the fact that the relief from this plague must come through social and economic progress, as much as through medical agencies. The improvement of living conditions and the popular dissemination of knowledge regarding sanitary and other preventive measures are agencies which strike at the source of the disease, and these are the factors which are emphasized all through the American exhibits. Travelling tuberculosis exhibitions, popular illustrated lectures, and the wide distribution of leaflets of information are effecting a revolution in the popular mind regarding tuberculosis.
You will notice that this' extract states again that the key note was prevention. That is what we are'advocating here; we are asking this government to give a sufficient sum each year to teach the people how to prevent this dread disease. ^Again we read in this magazine, on page 172:
In the moving of the exhibit from Washington to New York, figures of impressive size are once more given out. The bulk of the exhibit is measured in carloads, in more than a thousand of packing cases, in hundreds of exhibitors from four continents, and in tons of freight. The tuberculosis exhibit of 1908 equals in bulk the circus of a generation ago, when circuses first moved from town to town by railroad.
Governor Hughes and Mayor McClellan took part in "the programme of the opening night and there will be other special programmes for physicians, for the state, for the city and for neighbouring cities in New York and Long Island and New Jersey. The first folder announcing the exhibit will reach 25,000 homes and others following it will, it is planned, penetrate into every tenement in the city. Where thousands saw the exhibit in Washington hundreds of thousands will view it in New York.
So we say it is only reasonable that this government should develop a system of somewhat the same kind, in order to teach the people by travelling exhibits the danger of this disease and the way of combatting it. Now, to show the practical success that has attended this work, and the effect it is having in reducing the number of deaths, and in inspiring us with a hope that we may be able in future to extinguish the disease altogether, I wish to give a few figures. In England, Dr. William Parker, of the Westmoreland Consumptive Sanatorium, gives the following figures of actual results:
Deaths per Ten Thousand.
1851-55	 28 05
1861-65	 25-27
1871-75	 22-.18
1881-85	 18-30
1891-95	 14 62
1896-1900	 13-23

You will notice how the percentage reduces regularly in each term of five years, and it is estimated that if this decrease continues the disease will have entirely, disappeared by 1940. I ask why we cannot expect to accomplish such a result in this country when we consider that such a result has been obtained in other diseases- in the matter of leprosy, which was taken up by the Dominion government many years ago. In Denmark the fight against this disease was begun in 1895. According to Dr. H. T. Bulstrode the mortality rate in Copenhagen was 34-2 per ten thousand in 1870-4, and it fell to 16-6 in 1899-1901. It was less than one-half in 1901 what it was in 1874. In other towns of Denmark it fell from 25-2 per ten thousand to 13-1 per ten thousand. They have made a special effort in Germany to fight this disease and they have a great many ways and methods of doing it. I do not propose to weary the House with many figures concerning it, but I simply wish to gut on record the statement of Dr. Moeller regarding the sanatorium at Belzig that he is able to report from 12 to 15 per cent of absolute cures; 30 to 35 per cent of marked improvements, and 35 to 40 per cent of improvements; showing that in that sanatorium nearly 80 per cent have obtained considerable benefit. With regard to the general mortality in Prussia from tuberculosis, we find that in 1876 of every ten thousand persons there 30-95 per cent died of tuberculosis, in 1886	30-14, in 1896,	22 07
and in 1901, 19-54 per ten thousand. So much benefit has been obtained from this treatment that the German insurance societies have, in many cases, taken the matter up and have spent their own good money as they thought it would pay them to do so. According to the reports I find that from 1893 to 1901 they treated 5,814 persons of whom 1,228 died, 3,955 are now earning their own living and 630 could not afterwards bo_ traced. I find that Dr. Saar reported to the Washington congress that in the German army tuberculosis has been diminished by 42 per cent during the last 20 years simply by careful medical inspection and systematic precautions. Last year Dr. Phillip, an eminent authority on this subject, was here from Edinburgh and he stated that the measures taken in Edinburgh to prevent this disease had resulted in a reduction of 42 per cent in deaths in the ten years from 1897 to 1906. We know that right here in Ottawa very good work is being done. We have in this city a local association in which there are many men and women who have given a good deal of their time and money to assist in fighting this disease. What is the result? This association began in the year 1904 and during the last six years the deaths from tuberculosis have been as follows:

In other words they have fallen, in the last six years from 142 to 107. In the same period the city has kept growing, as.we all know. It is estimated now that it has a population of about 80,000, whereas, six years ago there were only 60,000. Taking the percentages of deaths we find that the ratio has fallen from 23-67 for every ten thousand people to 13-37. In other "words the deaths in this city are proportionately much less than they were six years ago. The number of cases taken care of outside the homes of the patients by this association in 1905 was 17; 1906, 41; 1907, 74; and 1908, 89. I give these figures out of fair play to the society in Ottawa. It has done much good work and one of the reasons why I am pleading with this government to increase its grant to the Canadian association is because the effect of the local work has been so good. This local association in Ottawa has arranged for an excellent system of visits by nurses, and it has also "made arrangements for giving free the advice and services of the medical profession at two different places in this city. At the present time it is building a large hospital for advanced cases of tuberculosis out near the experimental farm. This building is nearly finished and we expect to have it open in about a month. I think that the members of the local association would be very glad if members of parliament would take enough interest in it to go out, either by the street car or walking, some* afternoon and see the building which has been put up on the outskirts of the city for the care of advanced cases-of those unfortunate people who have hitherto had no place to go and who have been a source of contagion to their families and neighbours. I have here an extract from a report of Dr. Law the medical health officer for Ottawa for the year ending 31st October, 1908 He says:

subtopic: EXTRACTS FROM THE REPORT OF DR LAW, MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH, OTTAWA, FOR THE YEAR ENDING OCTOBER 31, 1908.

speechtext:
Six years ago scarlet fever held second place in the list of infectious diseases mortal-it_y with 50 deaths. This year it is in last place with but 2 deaths. (Population 6 years ago about 60,000 against 80,000 now).
Tuberculosis still maintains its proud supremacy as a life destroyer, apart from the sorrow and suffering it entails on the bereaved ones, many of whom are brought from comfort to poverty through the loss oi the household's provider after a long exhausting and expensive illness.
Contrasting the mortalities from these two
diseases and the respective measures for controlling them I do not think it will be denied that, if as efficient measures were provided for the fight against tuberculosis as are provided for scarlet fever and the latter disease were accorded the inadequate provisions meted out for tuberculosis, in 6 years the relative position of these two diseases in the mortality list would be reversed.
I read this as an expression of opinion from the health officer of the city of Ottawa who is an expert on this subject and who states that he has no doubt that tuberculosis could be eradicated from our midst as easily as scarlet! fever if the proper precautions were taken. Five years ago I had the honour of bringing this question before this House, and at that time a unanimous resolution was passed regarding it. At the same time it was brought up in the Senate and practically the same resolution was unanimously passed there. Up to that time the Dominion government had given $2,000 per annum to the Canadian Association for the Prevention of Tuberculosis. Some two years ago, after we had brought the matter to the attention of the government in several ways, the annual grant was raised to $5,000 per annum. This money was placed in the hands of the Canadian Association for the Prevention of Tuberculosis and was used by that association for the purpose of educating the people, disseminating information regarding this disease, its prevention and cure, and trying to stir up municipalities and provinces to take their share in this great work.
It has sometimes been said to me that we ought to raise money by private subscription to assist the Canadian association; in fact an important member of this government spoke to me privately about this some time ago. I am anxious to press upon the government that it would be exceedingly unwise for us to attempt to raise funds by private subscription to support the Canadian association. The Canadian association is entirely for the purpose of disseminating information by pamphlets and lectures and in any other way that it can in order to teach the people how they can protect themselves from this disease and how it can be cured. Any one who is willing to give money to help on this fight will give it to his local association. The Canadian association stirs up the people to put up a fight against this enemy. That necessitates the building of sanatoria or the establishment of local associations, a system of nurses, &c., in the different cities, all of which costs a great deal of money, and if the Canadian association arouses the people to the necessity of these steps it is accomplishing what it is established for. I claim that this government ought in all reason to make a grant sufficient to enable the Canadian association to do what is necessary to teach the people how to protect themselves or else

that this government should take hold of the question under the director of public health as a part of the work of that department of government. A good deal has been accomplished by this Canadian association which has now been in existence for several years. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller), who was last year president of this association, will be able to tell you all about it. As far as I am able to judge, the people are waking up regarding this important question, they are organizing locally in many places in Canada and they are being taught to work to help themselves in preventing this disease and in curing it when it has been contracted. The hospital which is being erected in Ottawa is costing between $45,000 and $50,000. This money has been raised entirely by private subscription. The City of Ottawa has undertaken to maintain this hospital but contributes nothing towards the building or its equipment. A small grant is given by the . Ontario government to assist in building such a hospital and of the balance I am proud to say that the ladies of Ottawa have raised quite a sum by a fair which they held in the drill hall a couple of years ago to which all classes of the community contributed and in which the household of the Governor General especially took an interest. The balance of the money which has been contributed by citizens of Ottawa I have had the pleasure and privilege of collecting. Already there is talk in Ottawa of attempting to establish a sanatorium for incipient cases. That will have to be in the country somewhere, but we all hope we will be able to arrange for it after the hospital for the advanced cases is firmly established.
I wish to press on the government that this Canadian association is purely for the purpose of disseminating information by lectures and pamphlets, and also to urge on the provincial governments and municipalities local action in this matter. The association now has a medical lecturer and unless the federal grant is increased we will not be able to keep up the work of sending out pamphlets and also to keep this lecturer on the road all the time as he ought to be. I ask that this government either take the matter in hand themselves or else give a sufficient grant to the Canadian association to enable it, with the greatest economy, to do the necessary work in this direction.
I have laid before you some of the results of this work, I have shown you how the mortality has decreased where proper precautions have been taken and how the work of the Canadian association here has led to the establishment of our hospital in Ottawa
My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) will tell you later on of other things Mr. PERLEY.
that have been done through the instrumentality of the Canadian association. I ask what possible objection there can be to this government granting sufficient money each year to this association to carry on this work properly. I can see no objection whatever. Five years ago when this matter [DOT] was brought up, a question was raised as to the propriety of this parliament doing anything, under the British North America Act. Even if that were a valid objection it would remind one of the action of a foolish man who was so careful of the rights of his neighbours that when his house was on fire he refused to jump out of his window because by doing so he would be committing a technical trespass on his neighbour's property. The argument that this would be an encroachment on the British North America Act would be as unreasonable as tha.t. But Sir, fortunately there is nothing in the British North America Act to prevent this parliament from taking action. It is true that under the British North America Act the sanatoria and hospitals are placed under the jurisdiction of the provinces. But public health as such is not mentioned in the British North America Act; in other words, it is_ under the Dominion and the provinces jointly. I need not go into this question in detail. It was discussed at a considerable length five years ago, when it was shown that in the early years of the Dominion there was on the statute-book a Public Health Act, under which action could be taken by the Dominion government to any extent that it saw fit. That Act was eventually repealed, but not because it was regarded as beyond our jurisdiction. The government has .already acknowledged that it has a perfect right to give money for this purpose, by granting $5,000 per annum. If the government can grant $5,000 it can grant $10,000 or $20,000 or whatever sum may be required to assist the fight against this dread disease. The hon. Minister of Agriculture this afternoon gave the amounts expended in protecting the human race from disease as against the amounts expended for protecting cattle and other animals. Where is the authority for this government expending such large sums of money in protecting cattle from disease? I fail to find it mentioned in the British North America Act. I did not catch the figures given by the minister this afternoon; but the expenditure in the four years from 1904 to 1907 inclusive in protecting the health of animals was stated last year, in answer to a question of mine, to have been $1,209,000; and this year the hon. minister of Agriculture has on the Order Paper a Bill entitled An Act to Prevent the Introduction or Spreading of Insects, Pests and Diseases Destructive to Vegetation, under which he is authorized 'to make regulations for the granting of

compensation for any crop, tree, bush or other vegetation or containers thereof so destroyed'. If this government can take such good care of the vegetable crops of this country, it seems to me that it ought to be able to grant assistance to protect human life from disease.
The humane considerations ought to be quite sufficient to justify action in this matter, and I apologize for suggesting the financial loss to the country resulting from tuberculosis. There are differences of opinion as to the amount of the loss from the death of each person. On this point Dr. Irving Fischer of Yale tells us:
The cost to the United States of every consumptive who dies is $8,000. That does not mean his sickness only and his funeral expenses. It includes the money he would have earned with the average ' expectation of life ' in the working years of which he is deprived, and adds to that the support of his family, which usually must be undertaken by some one else. Even conservative estimates rate the deaths from tuberculosis in 1906 at 138,000. A simple calculation, and we find that the United States lost in actual money used up, plus working nower destroyed, $1,100,000,000 during that year.
I do not place the actual loss as high as that, yet I must acknowledge that Dr. Irving Fischer knows a great deal more about it than I do. It is estimated that in Canada from 8,000 to 10,000 die annually from this disease. I have statistics only from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, which contains about 4,000,000 people, for the year 1907. These show that the total deaths in that year were : in Ontario, 33,502; in Quebec, 29,007; total, 62,509. Of these the deaths from tuberculosis were: in Ontario, 2,530; in Quebec, 2,884; a total of 5,414 in the two provinces. According to these figures, I estimate that in the Dominion of Canada from 8,000 to 10,000 people die of tuberculosis every year, and of these all the experts are agreed that we ought to be able to save fully half. To say nothing of the misery and suffering and trouble caused by this fell disease, think of the immense money loss which this Dominion suffers thereby. If Canada loses from 8,000 to 10,000 people annually from this disease, there must be in the country from 40,000 to 50,000 people suffering from it. Estimating each'life as worth $1,000, a most moderate estimate, and the loss resulting from the inactivity of the patient during the years he is ill at $1,000 moTe, that makes $2,000 for each life lost from this disease. On this basis this country loses from $16,000,000 to $20,000,000 annually from these deaths. Does this not furnish a strong reason, on the money basis alone, why this government should provide any reasonable amount required for the purpose of teaching the people how to protect themselves from this great annual loss? Why, Sir, ordinary common
sense should teach us that such prodigious waste ought to be stopped if at all possible, and I am glad to be able to say that in this case we know that it is possible.
This government spends large sums of money in bringing immigrants into this country. This year we have $915,000 in the estimates for this purpose, and we know that some of this money is wasted. I am not casting any reflection upon the immigrants when I say, what every one knows, that our own people in Canada are of more value to us than trie newcomers; and would it not pay us better to spend some money in saving our own people? The expenditure on immigration is supposed to be partly as an advertisement, to show what a fine country we have. I ask, would anv advertisement be so good for Canada as to show not only that we have a climate in which we can cope successfully against this fell disease, but that we have a people and a government wise enough to take advantage of their opportunities and to put up a fight against it?
When this question was under discussion five years ago, the hon. Minister of Agriculture remarked that no one had suggested how the government could spend money on this object without trespassing on the rights of the provinces. This is a simple question. The provinces are building sanatoria and hospitals, and this parliament has not only the right but the duty to spend money in fighting this disease in any other way. For instance, this government could promote the dissemination of information by means of pamphlets or lectures. We have already had one lecturer at work a part of the time, but there is room in this broad Dominioin for a man to be at work every day in the year, promoting the formation of local associations to build hospitals and fight this disease in the various cities and towns.
It has been suggested in some quarters that an official physician should be appointed by the Dominion government, to take cognizance of this disease, to keep statistics concerning it, and if considered wise, later to arrange a system of inspection and registration. Of course, this appointment would come under the authority of the Dominion if they saw fit to make it. Then, there is one way in which we could help a great deal in fighting this disease, in a practical every-day way, and that is in connection with railways and steamboats. No steps have been taken, so far as I know, by any authority to try to keep down the contagion in these public conveyances. That is a matter that would naturally come directly under the authority of this government. Then, we have this magazine from which I have read. I wonder if there is any reason why this government should not have such a publi-

cation which could be distributed throughout this Dominion, giving facts and figures with regard to this disease, as well as other matters of a kindred nature in order to teach people something which they ought to know for their own protection. Then a public exhibition such as that concerning which I read as having been held in New York and which was afterwards used as a travelling exhibit in many parts of the United States, is a homely, every-day way of teaching the people how to prevent this disease and how to cure it. That is something that would certainly come absolutely within the authority of the Dominion government, something with which the provinces would have nothing to do. The provinces have plenty to do, and so have the municipalities, but this general work ought to be done by the Dominion government.
I merely mention these things to show that there are many ways in which the hon. Minister of Agriculture can spend money in this good work without even technically violating the British North America Act. I am not wedded to any particular plan or method, but I feel strongly that this government should take prompt and serious action, in whatever direction it thinks best, to help the people to fight this grim enemy. In the session of 1905, a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons brought in a report on this matter indicating what further steps should be taken to suppress tuberculosis in this country. The committee had held several meetings, and on July 13, 1905, I had the honour to present its report in this House. That report was discussed here, and adopted, except that, at the suggestion of the government section 7 was struck out, which section, if I remember well, provided for a grant of money. In this report, as passed, section 8 reads as follows:
Your committee further suggests that unless the Dominion government feels prepared to take hold of the matter itself, a conference should be held at as early a date as possible between the federal and provincial authorities for the purpose of determining the best action which should be taken in the premises.
That report was passed unanimously. But no conference has been held. And, without finding fault too severely with the government for not carrying out this report,
I submit that it would have been wiser had this conference been called. What we want is to get everybody working on this problem. If we have the conference-and I would urge the government to call one- it could not but be productive of good.
I do not wish to weary the House with this matter. I do not think there is a greater or more important question before the country to-day, and I believe that if Mr. PEBLEY.
the people thoroughly understood it this parliament would be forced to spend every cent that was required to put up a good hard fight against this disease. I hope that the discussion of this resolution will help the public to understand this question. I trust that our friends of the press will give it space in their papers, not on my account, but on account of the vitally important interests involved. This is not, in any sense, a local question.. This disease is spread all over the Dominion, and people suffering from it move from one section to another. The number of deaths caused by it is so great that the need of fighting it is imperative. And we must get the help, not only of those individuals who are willing to help, not only of the municipalities, but also the great .strength of this Dominion government must be brought to assist if the fight is going to be a success. We know that our climate is as favourable to the cure of this disease as any other, if the disease is taken in time. And I am glad to say that, through the information that has been disseminated throughout the country during the last few years, the people are beginning to understand the question, they are waking up to the difficulties involved, and also they are learning to feel that it is perfectly possible to destroy this disease altogether if we make a united effort. At this time the Dominion government has a large revenue. It is making great expenditures, some of which are criticised by those of us who sit on this side of the House. It seems to me that here is a case in which the government can make a grant which no one will criticise, but with which every one will be satisfied, and which will accomplish much good for the people of the whole Dominion. I do not suggest in any way that this government should take in hand the building of sanatoria or hospitals of any kind, but I do feel that they should spend sufficient money to teach the people of tliis country 1'ow to prevent and cure this disease. I do not think that any practical or theoretical objection wmuld be raised to the spending of this money to protect ourselves and our children. And I say in conclusion that this parliament represents the common sense and wisdom of this Canada of ours, and if we do not put up a proper fight against this scourge of our day and generation, we shall be held responsible before the world of public opinion for neglect of a plain duty.

subtopic: EXTRACTS FROM THE REPORT OF DR LAW, MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH, OTTAWA, FOR THE YEAR ENDING OCTOBER 31, 1908.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of the prevention and cure of tuberculosis has been considered in this House on several previous occasions. The hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) alone has already had on the order paper two resolutions in

reference to this matter. My hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Black) also took the matter up, though in another form, two years ago. However, to my mind, a question such as this cannot be often and too carefully considered, and too great pressure cannot be brought to bear on the government in this connection.
Already, on a previous occasion, I have clearly expressed my views, both as a physician a.nd as a representative of the people, on this very live question. There is too much force and eloquence in the grim and cold facts or statistics submitted by the hon. member to make it necessary that I should dilate at any length on the sufferings brought about by the scourge of tuberculosis. After what has been so clearly and so neatly stated by the mover of the resolution, it only remains for me to approve of the conclusion laid down in regard to the grant in favour of the anti-tuberculosis association.
Indeed it would be regrettable were Canada, a leader in so many branches of industrial and commercial activity, to sadly lag behind when confronted with a social and economical problem of such importance. All civilized countries have realized what enormous losses result from the spread of tuberculosis, and have applied preventive and curative measures of the greatest efficiency.
The Dominion government has made a good beginning, but it behoves all members of this House who like myself belong to the medical profession to make official quarters ring with the necessity, in the country's interest, of preventing the spread of tuberculosis, and particularly of tuberculosis of the lungs.
I am of opinion, as previously stated, that a certain amount should be deducted from the items appropriated directly or indirectly towards forwarding immigration, and an equal amount spent towards the prevention and cure of tuberculous diseases. To my mind, more value should be attached from our country's standpoint, to saving the life of one Canadian snatched from the grip of tuberculosis, than to securing an immigrant from foreign shores, whatever his worth.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we have before us a question of the greatest import both from the economical and humanitarian standpoint; and I trust that the government, desirous of forwarding the best interests of the country, will find their way to granting a still larger appropriation to the men who have assumed the task of putting a stop, in this country, to what is sometimes termed the wdiite plague.

subtopic: EXTRACTS FROM THE REPORT OF DR LAW, MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH, OTTAWA, FOR THE YEAR ENDING OCTOBER 31, 1908.
speechtext:
This is a subject that ought to give, and I have no doubt does give, every member of this House both interest and pleasure. It is a ques-1
tion for humanity, one of those subjects in which one side of the House will not disagree with the other, but in which we all unite for humanity's sake. And the pleasantest part is that such an interest and such an. initiative is being shown by the laymen. It has not been left to the medical profession alone to do this work, but the laymen, in many instances, have outstripped the medical profession in their earnest work for the protection of the lives .of our people against this sad destroyer. I would express my appreciation and gratitude for what this government has done year by year in fighting this disease. I regard this matter in no spirit of fault-finding, complaining or scolding, but rather in a spirit of gratitude for what has been done; and I believe we shall be, in the future, under a still greater debt of gratitude to the government, for I am sure they will respond to the request of the Anti-tuberculosis Association for some greater grant than has been given in the past.
I think it is right, in asking for a greater grant than we have had in the past, to review what has been done with the grants that have been given. Have we been doing good work? Have we been expending this money as it should have been expended? Let us see what has been done. For one thing, literature, in plain language that the unlearned might understand and that all might read, has been scattered broadcast all over Canada. This has been a great means of teaching the people how to protect themselves against this disease. Over and above that, we have a lecturer who goes all over Canada lecturing to the people on this subject. I think this is one of the most interesting and profitable means of combatting this dread disease. At present the travelling lecturer of the association is a medical gentleman of culture, an expert in discussing the prevention of tuberculosis, a man who has the ability to stand on the platform and interest the general public in the question. I believe that up to the present time he has gone over many portions of Canada. Speaking for my own province of what the lecturer has done, I may say that I had the great pleasure of arranging for him a series of meetings from Windsor to Yarmouth, where there were crowded houses at every meeting, where not only the educated, the intelligent and the cultured assembled to listen, but where the common people heard him gladly; and I think that was the most promising part of it. Not alone is information imparted by the lecturer, but in each place that the lecturer visits, an association is formed for the prevention of tuberculosis, and in many cases active working committees are formed for the spread of knowledge how to prevent tuberculosis. More than that, local medical men are giving lectures in their own communities and

in neighbouring communities. There are very few medical men, I hope there are none, who cannot stand up and intelligently instruct an audience in the details for the prevention of this disease, so far as those details are known to-day. *
I may say that over and above what has been said in regard to tuberculosis, over and above the spread of Knowledge how to prevent this disease, the enlightenment has not ended there, but it has gone beyond the bounds of the object first intended, and the knowledge of the prevention generally of all disease has been spread throughout the country. People have learned, not only how to prevent tuberculosis, but in learning how to prevent that they have also learned a better mode of living. More sunlight is entering the homes of our people, more fresh air is entering their houses, and a more sensible mode of preparing and eating our food, is being adopted, while a better knowledge of hygienic laws has been spreading all over the country. Now the question is being asked, if we can prevent tuberculosis, why can we not prevent other diseases? Interest has been awakened all over this continent, and in many parts of Europe, not only in the prevention of tuberculosis, but in the prevention of other diseases as well. This of course is beyond what was intended by the anti-tuberculosis association, but it is'a fact that the good work has gone beyond the bounds that were first measured out for it by the society. In the United States the light has spread abroad so much that men of wealth are devoting their means to the prevention, not only of tuberculosis, but of other diseases. We read in the newspapers an announcement that Mrs. Russell Sage has donated a million dollars in aid of the campaign against tuberculosis. That would have been an astonishing thing ten or fifteen years ago, but it shows how public interest is being aroused, and how men of means are turning their attention to this philanthrophic work. We also read that Mr. John D. Rockefeller has promised that he will give a million dollars to combat the hook-worm, which is a very destructive disease in the southern states, and that Mr. Andrew Carnegie will give a like amount towards battling pellagra, which is another disease carrying off many thousands in the southern states. Thus you will see that from the point where the anti-tuberculosis association began, the good work has gone on until it is spreading all over this continent and all over the world.
But this is only a sample of what has been done. Since the anti-tuberculosis societies have g;ot to work the question has been asked over and over again, not only, how can we prevent that disease, but how can we prevent other diseases, how can we save human life? For instance, atten-Mr. BLACK.
tion is now turning strongly toward the prevention of the slaughter of the innocents, the alarming and unnecessary deaths of little children, not only from tuberculosis but from ignorant care. There is nothing probably in Canada that is so decimating little children as ignorance in feeding them. The death rate among children in Canada is greater than any other death rate, and we might class the various diseases almost under one head, ignorance in feeding. There are every year over 31, 000 deaths of little children under five years of age. According to statistics in Canada, there are more deaths of children under five years of age, that is, more people die under five years of age, than die from the fifth to the fiftieth year. Much is being done through the interest awakened by the anti-tuberculosis association to prevent the enormous destruction of life in little children. In the city of New York a renowned philanthrophist, Mr. Nathan Strauss, has established milk depots to furnish pasteurized milk, in many cases for nothing, in many cases at cost price, to every one who wants it, and the health department of New York claim that he has reduced infant mortality in New York one-half. '
I have a clipping here from a Montreal paper of March, 1907. This is just an average statement that I happened to run against. [DOT] In March, 1907, in Montreal, in one week, there were 114 deaths; of these 114 deaths 103 were of children under five years of age. That is a terrible and unnecessary slaughter. The Guelph, Ontario, health officer reports 110 per thousand children died there against 11 per thousand of total deaths. That is an awful thing, but unfortunately, it is true. In Paris, so anxious have they become to save the lives of children, that they not only send out instructions to mothers how to feed and care for their children, but they have established depots all over the city where noor mothers, those below the poverty line, may go and have all the food they want to eat as many times a day as they please. The only requirement is that she is a mother and is, nursing her babe. The French government appreciate the necessity of preserving the lives of their people and they have taken this step amongst the poorest. All over the city of Paris they [DOT] have established these depots for the feeding of nursing mothers. The same care is being taken in other countries as well.
