subtopic: EXTRACTS FROM THE REPORT OF DR LAW, MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH, OTTAWA, FOR THE YEAR ENDING OCTOBER 31, 1908.
speechtext:
I know that Toronto is taking steps in that direction but we have no statistics from that city. I am speaking of these things as the result of the light being spread by the anti-tuberculosis associations of the country. I want to show that they have gone beyond what they first intended, fortunately, and that the whole world is being educated up to the prevention of disease. Prevention, prevention, everywhere! That is something that has been done and it is a grand record. We have to thank our government for what they have assisted us in doing in Canada. Another question would be: Is this a paying investment? The government gave us last year $5,000. Have they got interest for their money? I think, from the local knowledge that many of us have, and judging from the local work done that the government have not only received good interest for their money but have received compound interest. Not only do I believe that they have received compound interest but I believe that the debt of $5,000 has been paid and that the government are deeply indebted to the antituberculosis association of Canada. I want to repeat that I believe that not only has this investment been a good one but I believe that in the matter of dollars and cents, in saving wage earners, in saving people to help to build up this country, the government of Canada-the peonle of Canada-are indebted to the anti-tuberculosis association for the great work they have done. I hope the government will not only give twice $5,000 this year but that they will increase the grant each year. I think we have shown that a great work has been done and I think we have shown that it is a grand investment for the government. What more should be done? I think that, in consideration of what they have done in -checking the spread of tuberculosis, in consideration of the great good they have done not only in the fighting of this disease but in the spreading of knowledge for the prevention of other diseases, the government acknowledge their duty to the country to send out information instructing the people how to protect themselves. It has been stated by the gentleman who moved this motion that the government have expended a great deal of money in preserving the lives of domestic animals. They have and I think every dollar has been well spent. Half a million was spent last year, or the year before, and I do not think any body will find any fault with it or will say that it was not a profitable investment yielding good interest. But, if the government feel the responsibility of protecting and preserving the lives of domestic animals, surely the government
must feel their responsibility in preserving the lives of the people, and I think the time has come when the government should, in a more systematic way, take ud this question of public health, either by forming a bureau of public health, which, I believe, is the proper course,, or by starting in the direction of teaching the people how to preserve the public health. The hon. gentleman who moved this motion laid considerable stress upon the work done in publishing pamphlets and circulating them all over the country. Why not the government appoint a special agent to publish pamphlets on the prevention of other diseases? Why not teach communities that there is no need of having typhoid fever? Why not teach municipalities that it is a disgrace to have typhoid fever? Why not teach the people that small-pox, typhoid fever, measles, scarlet fever, whooping cough and all diseases of that class are unnecessary and preventable? We have fairly driven smallpox out of Canada. We have driven typhoid out of many communities. We have lessened the death rate of all these diseases and no one will gainsay the reasonable possibility of driving out of this country all these preventable diseases if the proper steps were taken. Would it not be money well invested if $5,000 or $10,000 were expended in distributing pamphlets all over Canada instructing the people how to preserve their health and how to prevent these diseases? The day has long gone by when the old verdict 'died by the visitation of God' is indulged in. We know that people die in many instances when there is no necessity of their dying. Of course, all men have to die, but the unnecessary loss of life among the wage earners and producers at the producing time of their life is immense. Would it not pay the government, would it not be a good investment, casting aside all the humanitarianism of it to adopt some systematic mode of teaching the people how to save their own lives? As the previous speaker (Mr. Perley) has said, we expend a lot of money in bringing immigrants into this country and we do that rightly, every one will commend the exertions of the government in bringing people into Canada, for we need them; but how much more .sensible, how much better, to save the lives of our own people? Thirty-one thousand infants die every year, one-half of whom, according to expert evidence, might be saved; and I think that is a small proportion, more than one-half might be saved. Add to that the tens of thousands who die of typhoid or other diseases in middle life or earlier manhood. Think ot all this enormous loss which is being permitted without an effort on the part of the government to stop it, yet we are spend-

ing money in bringing foreigners in to take the places of those who die.
It is sometimes said that this is the work of the provincial governments. I do not know where that theory has come from. I have looked over' the British North America Act and find nothing there to justify it. When that Act was framed, very little progress had been made in state sanitation, in state medicine in public health. I think the first active organized step taken on this continent was a state society or board of health formed in Massachusetts when I was a student in college in 1863. Only two references to public health occur in the British North America Act. One defines what the provinces are to do and the other what is within the -jurisdiction of the Dominion. The Dominion has quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals. To the provincial government is allotted the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities, eleemosynary institutions in and for the province other than marine hospitals. There is no further reference to public [DOT]health. In the United States form of government anvthing that is not expressed as belonging to the federal government goes to the state government. In Canada the exact opposite prevails, what is not mentioned as belonging to the provinces, belongs to the federal government. Therefore, I maintain it is the duty of the federal government to take such steps as will protect the health of the people. At the same time there it no necessity of interfering with the rights and the work of the provincial governments. The federal government is doing many things for the benefit of its people that are also being done by the provincial governments, and I do not know that they ever clash. Both are doing their work in agriculture and in many other things. To advance this constitutional difficulty seems like shirking a duty, like hunting for an excuse, like the argument that the Levite might have used when he found the poor fellow wounded and suffering by the wayside. He might have said: I belong to a tribe whose duty it is to perform religious ceremonies only; I am not here to attend to the fallen, it it not my work, the man probably has friends or relatives somewhere-and so he passed by on the other side. How much better for the government to take the course of the Samaritan who came along that way. I think he was a country doctor, by the way, because he was poor and had only a few coppers in his pocket, but he had a big heart in his body and he took up the poor fellow, he did not wait to say: This fellow may not be deserving and it is not my place to look after him anyway, he probably has friends some-Mr. BLACK.
where. He assisted him as far as he was able with first aid to the wounded and then took him to the first hotel he came to. Like many another country doctor he had not much to pay his board, so he ran his face for the man's board for several days until he might come back again. How much better for the government to take that course, helping in this great cause of humanity.
I have no doubt this is coming, I have no doubt we will have the government of Canada, as well as the local governments, taking hold of this great work of assisting the people to preserve their lives. I hope this -question will be discussed during the evening session, I hope that not only every medical man in this House will support the member for Argenteuil in his resolution, but that as many laymen as medical men will urge this thing and not forget that there are other diseases besides tuberculosis, in preventing which this government should assist.
At six o'clock the1 House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: EXTRACTS FROM THE REPORT OF DR LAW, MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH, OTTAWA, FOR THE YEAR ENDING OCTOBER 31, 1908.
speechtext:
Now, we have heard a great deal about the British North America Act standing in the way and preventing us from taking up this work as a Dominion work. I think that argument has been effectually disposed of by the hon. members who preceded me. This British North America Act is held up as a bugaboo, it is treated as an excuse for us to unload our responsibilities, or a portion of our responsibilities, upon the provincial authorities. I do not see why we should allow this to scare us away from our duties, or why we should plead it as an excuse. Illustrations have been given here to-day of the way in which the officials of this government act in concert with those of the governments of the several provinces in matters relating to education. Now, education is a subject that is relegated solely to the control of the provinces by the British North America Act, but consider such a matter, for instance, as the education of the farmer. Go to a meeting of a farmers' institute, and there on the same platform you will find a Dominion government official from one of the experimental farms who is there to assist in educating the farmer in the best way to carry on some of the many operations of the farm, and also some professor sent out under the auspices of the provincial authorities to carry on the work of education. These two officials work together, there is no clashing of authority, no question is raised by the provincial authorities that the Dominion government must keep off its preserve and must leave education wholly to the provinces. They are only too glad to share their responsibility. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) will know full well that a few years ago the question of looking after the health of animals was, in some provinces at least, wholly in the hands of the provincial authorities. But a mutual understanding was arrived at between the officials of the Minister of Agriculture and the officials of the provinces and this was handed over to the Dominion government, though, prior to that time, it had been thought a matter wholly within the jurisdiction of the province. The leader of the opposition (Mr. K. L. Borden) referred to cases in which assistance was given by this government to railways working under provincial charter. And so we could go on giving illustration after illustration to show that there has been invasion of the provincial domain without objection from the provincial authorities. This fight against tuberculosis should be a national affair. There will be no jealousy, no cry of provincial rights or anything of that nature from the provincial governments if the Dominion government desires to come in and lend a helping hand. We hear it stated that the Dominion government should not build sanatoria or hospi-Mr. EOCHE.
tals. That may be very true. But the Dominion government can render assistance to such institutions in operation. There are to-day at least two hospitals that are managed under civic authority-those at Winnipeg and St. Boniface-that receive money grants from the Dominion parliament. Why? Because immigrants are brought in by the Dominion government and dumped in the 'city of Winnipeg, and the Dominion authorities do not think it right or fair that the whole expense of treating and looking after those immigrants who need hospital care should devolve upon provincial or civic authorities. The Dominion recognizes that it has a duty to perform, and so it aids these hospitals by money grants year after year. We are carrying on a propaganda in the provinces to-day. They are doing good work by means of distribution of literature and by lectures. In this and other ways, many of the provinces are doing their full duty. Besides, we have our medical associations, and, philanthropists as they always are, the medical men are discharging their duty in the matter by getting out pamphlets on the disease and having them widely distributed. The good done by the central anti-tuberculosis association has been referred to by the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley). It is a good work. I think $5,000 is entirely too small a sum to enable that board to discharge the functions that they have been trying to discharge during the last two years, at any rate I would certainly favour an increased amount for the central association. But, in addition to all this, we require the united and hearty co-operation of the Dominion government. If we do not wish to go into the sanatoria business ourselves

and I am not urging the government to do so at the present time-we would assist those sanatoria now in operation by giving them grants according to population of the hospitals or by giving grants outright as they do in the case of the Winnipeg and St. Boniface hospitals.
There are many things this government might do in addition to improving sanitary conditions. I will refer to one of them, and I have already refered to it when speaking on this subject in years past. I think we ought to have a Dominion laboratory in this country where our young men could enjoy the opportunities for experimentation that are afforded in other countries. Is it not rather humiliating to think that in a nation like Canada, her young men have to go abroad to find under a foreign flag a scope for their talents, where they are enabled to experiment in the preparation of serums, anti-toxins, and such drugs which we have to import from England, or Germany, or the United States? If we were alive to our owm duty u'e should provide scope for our own young men, and w'e would

have the serums manufactured within the confines of our own country. I commend these few remarks to the House, and especially to the Minister of Agriculture. I tiust the Dominion government will grapple with this question with a little more vigour than they have shown in the past. While 1 commend them for what they have done in the past, I think that a much wider field lies open before them full of opportunities, end I would urge upon them to take into their serious consideration this subject with a view of meeting more fully than in the past the urgent demands of the country in this matter.

subtopic: EXTRACTS FROM THE REPORT OF DR LAW, MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH, OTTAWA, FOR THE YEAR ENDING OCTOBER 31, 1908.
speechtext:
I do not intend to take up much time in discussing this subject. One splendid feature of the debate so far is that the speeches have been so short; that is a plan which I very much favour in the discussion of all subjects. I think we are indebted to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Perley) who introduced this motion, and who introduced the same subject four or five years ago. I propose in my remarks to took at the subject from a little different point of view than that from which other hon. gentlemen have chosen to regard it. I do not think any medical man, or any layman, need make an apology to this House for taking up -some time in discussing this great question. My hon. friend from Argent-euil made many pertinent remarks, but none was more pertinent than when he said that if the people of this country were familiar, as they should be, with the ravages -of this -disease, the government would be compelled to act. I think that is an absolute fact. When we realize that in Canada to-day there are from 50,000 to 60,000 people affected with tuberculosis, and that from 10,000 to 12,000 are dying annually, the -subject assumes tremendous importance. Especially do we become impressed in view of tire well established fact to-day that tuberculosis is not only a preventable disease, but it is a curable disease. I know it is very difficult to make the people believe that, it will be difficult to make many members of this House believe it. Any medical man in this country "who has practised for some time will tell you that when a patient comes to us for physical examination with the slightest idea that he is affected with tuberculosis, it takes a 'good deal of courage on -our part to give the patient a straight -diagnosis. We have always felt in our practice that once we declare the patients to be tubercular, or to have consumption, as the term is, they pretty nearly always abandon hope; there is no question about that. Now, if medical science has done nothing more than to restore hope m the breast of the patient, it has certainly done a great -deal already, for any physi-'	45
cian is ready to admit that hope is one of the greatest aids we have in the medical profession.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it may seem a strange thing to say that tuberculosis is curable, or that it is preventable. But that is a fact established centuries ago. In the first centuries the best medical men held that this disease was contagious, that it could be communicated from -one person to another; they went further, and they said that the best means of curing it was fresh air. Now we have got but very little beyond that state of affairs to-day. I think there is no medical man in Canada who pretends to prescribe medicine now to his tubercular patients; he advises them to live out of doors, and that is the reason why the idea of the sanatorium lia3 arisen and has taken so much extension. They went further in olden times, and ws find that in the fifteenth century they used means which we do not often use to-day, but which we should use to a greater extent than we do. If a patient died of tuberculosis -or consumption, as it was then termed, the clothing and the -bed-clothing had to be destroyed. Now -certainly that is an evidence -of the -belief that tuberculosis is preventable or curable. The question then arises in our minds, how is it that, if this belief has been prevalent -during all those centuries, we have not made more progress in -our treatment of the disease? In regard to the sanatoria in -Canada, I think perhaps we have -done as much as most other countries, considering that we are a new country. I remarked a little while ago that from 50,000 to 60,000 people in this country were affected with tuberculosis, and yet in spite of all that the provinces have done, they have only beds for about 500 patients.
1 have a list of the provinces, but I will not read it. It is enough to say that in the whole Dominion there are only -beds for about 500 patients.
Now it is established that the treatment patients receive in the sanatorium is the only kind that holds out much hope for them as a cure of tuberculosis. What is to .become of all the others? And just at that point comes in the work of the association of which my hon. friend who introduced this motion was talking to-day, in connection with the education of the people. He has given you a pretty clear idea of what that association is doing in an educational way. I just refer to that to point out that we have only provided for 500 persons and to ask what we are going to do for the rest. I have had a little experience with tuberculosis and I have looked into the experience of some of the best men of this country. I say that spieh-did results can be achieved outside of a sanatorium. The same kind of treatment is required inside and outside of a sana-

toiium. Persons should be instructed to sleep outdoors, to sleep on the verandah.
I live in a fairly cold country and some people may say: Surely your patients cannot sleep outdoors in Manitoba? I have patients with whom I have achieved great success in my own practice. I might also refer you to Dr. Bell, one of the best bacteriologists of this country, an honest man, and he cures a great many patients by having' them sleep, during even this winter, on the verandah. That is one point that this association should impress upon the people. They should instruct them that if they cannot go to a sanatorium they can take the same kind of treatment. I have very carefully read the speech that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) made five years ago on this subject and for fear that I may misquote him I want to refer to a few sentences which he used. I wonder if he has read over this speech carefully since he made it. It is in the minister's department that this matter is placed and I would like to have more faith that the minister is in earnest in connection with this great question, but I look upon this speech of his as more the speech of the politician than of the statesman, as trying to evade the question by having recourse to the British North America Act, trying to get all out of that Act that can be got out of it in connection with this most important subject. He says:
I would point out that up to the present time no scheme has been put forward by those who are interested and who form this association which they could lay before the government or before parliament to indicate in w hat way such work as that might be improved, extended or rendered more effective.
If he had any excuse along that line when he spoke before, I think the hon. gentleman who introduced this motion to-day has taken that excuse from him, and I just wondered when my hon. friend was speaking what kind of a speech he would make to-night in reference to that point. They may not have done all they could. I am of the opinion that there are too many academic speeches on this as on many other subjects, and I want to get down to practical facts. I think, in the short time at my disposal, that I can show the minister that, notwithstanding how hard and fast the British North America Act may be, there are lines along which this government can act and do as much good as if the British North America Act in this respect was wide open.
It is quite possible that the association for preventing the spread of tuberculosis may be able to provide that information. ... It would be impossible, I think, for me or any other member of the government to decide or to say what we ought to do or what we could do until some detail of a scheme of the kind were laid before parliament and before the , Mr. SCHAFFNER.
government, but we think that it would be in the interest of the people at large that those who are to-day giving their attention to this work should turn their attention most particularly to devising something which ought be done under the authority and through the intervention of this parliament.
I think that the hon. gentleman who introduced this motion has made that right.
To the Dominion is given by the British North America Act the establishment and maintenance of quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals.
The Minister of Agriculture will go no further than that. Well, let us take him at his word. But, before I refer to that, a contrast was drawn in the_ House this afternoon between those countries that have adopted the outdoor treatment for the cure of tubercular patients and those countries which have paid no attention to outdoor treatment. In England, in 1891, about 224 people in ten thousand died of tuberculosis. To-dav in England they cure about fifty per cent of the patients, and instead of having 22i deaths in ten thousand they have about half that number. Portugal, which has done verv little for the relief oi its people in this connection and which has a population of 4,500,000, loses about
20,000	people annually from tuberculosis. I do not think it is necessary for me to call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to anv other instances. There are two bald cases. One has adopted the outdoor treatment and the results are apparent. I believe that this government have a duty to perform no matter what view they take of the British North America Act, and I am going to refer to a few of the wavs in which that duty can be carried out. Tuberculosis to-day is considered to be a contagious disease which can be communicated from one to the other. I admit that there is perhaps too much stress laid upon the question of the sputum or that which the tubercular patient spits out and which, becoming dry, is disseminated and breathed in by other people. No doubt that is the most prominent way of communicating the disease, but there are many other wavs. When a patient coughs, the moisture which is discharged into the atmosphere certainlv is a means of contagion. Living in ill-ventilated rooms, poor food, insufficient clothing, anything that reduces the constitution of the individual, is a means of inducing tuberculosis. My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) referred to the milk supply. That is a more important question than this country has yet realized. We have found that tubercular bacilli are not affected very much by the gastric juices of the stomach. The bacillus still remains in such a condition that it is able to do a great deal of damage

to the child or person who has drunk it. It seems to be absorbed into the glandular system. While the results along that line are not very clear there is still a great deal of opinion that we contract tuberculosis from eating the meat of tubercular animals. My hon. friend from Grev (Mr. Miller) asked a question along that line, and I may be anticipating what he wishes to demonstrate by saying that this government have spent more in guarding animal life than they have on humanity. I do not care how much they spend in protecting domestic animals from disease, if in all cases the money is spent judiciously and to the best advantage; but I believe that we should take even more pains than we have bestowed on the cattle we import into this country in the protection of human life. In relation to cattle we have to-day the tuberculin, test, by which we may ascertain absolutely that the food of which we partake is free from tuberculosis. Having that test, money is no consideration; at any cost we must be sure that our food, our meat and milk are free from tuberculosis.
But let us for a moment consider other methods by which the federal government can do great work in preventing tuberculosis. It has been said that if we are to grapple with this great subject we need an intelligent people, expert physicians and wise governments. Look to-day at the army and navy, where you have intelligent official superintendence of the health of men. Fewer cases of tuberculosis develop in the army and navy of Great Britain than in any other set of men. Why? No man can enter either the army or navy until he passes a satisfactory physical examination by a medical man and he is examined from time to time after enlisting; he must be physically healthy or he is not permitted to remain a member of the army or navy. Let our government apply that same principle m every department of its administration, and I am not sure that it will not do as much to prevent tuberculosis as all the sanatoria of this country are doing to-day. Take, for example, the opportunity'that lies before the government in the prevention of tuberculosis among Indians. We have in Canada to-day about 375 bands of Indians with a population of about 110,000. Every one knows that the Indian is four times as susceptible to tuberculosis as the white man. In the west the Indians generally wander over the country, in Ontario they live a more settled life and in Ontario they do not spread the disease to the same extent as in the Northwest. A little is being done for the Indians, but very little. Surely the British North America Act does not prevent the Minister of the Interior from having his officials ascertain who among the Indians are affected with this disease 45}
and seeing that they are segregated or kept from the other Indians, so that they are not spitting over the prairies with the chance that the sputum will be licked up by animals, absorbed into the glands and cause tubercular beef.
Let us look at the great department of the post office of this country. No other department of the government comes so closely in contact with the people as the Post Office Department. There is scarcely a person in Canada who does not have something to do with letters or papers handled by the post office. There are today almost 4,000 clerks in the post office of Canada. No one of these officers who handles tlm mails should be permitted to discharge his duties without having passed a physical examination for tuberculo.sis just as he would have to do in the Militia Department. There is great danger of the mail bags becoming contaminated with tubercular bacilli. At every station great bags of mail too heavy to be carried, are thrown from the mail car and dragged along and across the platform. Perhaps just before the mail bag is thrown on the platform a tubercular patient may have spat on the platform and I am almost afraid to say that one tubercular patient can expectorate seven billion tubercular bacilli in one day. Tubercular patients are not confined to bed in the earlier stages and in the small towns, as they have not much to do, they are likely to be found around the station at train time, so that this danger is a very real one. I would suggest to the government that they should have disinfecting stations for mail bags on the Atlantic and on the Pacific coast and also at one or more central points. It may be said that the mail is inside the bags, But as this economical government keeps patching these bags year after year and in sending them for repairs pack nineteen bags in one bag, the outside of each of these bags may contaminate the containing bag. Surely the British North America Act would not prevent these simple precautions in the Post Office Department, the disinfecting of mail bags and the physical examination of the men and women who handle the mail that goes into the families of different countries.	,
I am about to make a statement which I believe to be exceedingly important, but which I hesitate to make for fear of being suspected of unfair criticism. I may say, by way of preface, that I know very few civil servants in this country and that in the statement I am about to make I have no reference to any particular case. We have heard a great deal about isolating tubercular patients. We isolate small-pox and scarlet fever patients and we will never get rid of tuberculosis until we look on it just as we do on small-pox and scarlet

fever. I am told that in the departments in Ottawa there are tubercular patients. If persons suffering from tuberculosis are likely to do harm on the farm, how much more harm are the'y likely to do where a great number of young men and young women, at the very age when they are most susceptible to this disease, are brought into contact with each other in their daily work. I am told that there are quite a few persons in the Civil Service of this town who are afflicted with tuberculosis in an advanced stage. If that condition of affairs exists, I say, with all sympathy for those who are afflicted, that it is a condition of affairs that should be remedied at once. If these civil servants are not in a position to take care of themselves, the government should do something for them; and I am prepared to support the expenditure of any amount of money for this purpose, for money is no object in dealing' with this great problem. But these persons should not, because they are poor or are deserving of our sympathy, be allowed to mingle from day to day with young men and young women who are free from that disease. This is another direction in which the British North America Act does not prevent the Minister of Agriculture working.
I am not going to discuss the Immigration Department. The Minister of the Interior is not here, and I do not want to say anything to which he would not have an opportunity to reply; but I have reason to believe that all the tuberculosis patients are not turned back, but a good many come in.
I feel that there is no subject that more deserves the attention of this House than this very question I have tried to suggest some methods by which the government could improve the present condition of affairs. I am strongly of the opinion that we should have in this country a bureau of health as a separate department. There is no other department so important. It seems strange that up to the present time the great country to the south of us has not had a bureau of health; but I am glad to observe that President Taft realized the importance of the subject and proposes that the United States shall have a bureau of health under a separate minister. Whether or not Canada could go just that far today I am not prepared to say, but I believe that is what we should aim at. The provinces are doing a great deal in this matter, and I am pleased to have a couple of photographs to show the Minister of Agriculture and other members of the government what the province of Manitoba is doing in this work. We shall have completed in about a month an institution with 50 beds. .
Now, this motion says:

further lessen the great suffering and mortality caused by this disease.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate for the sole and only purpose of acquainting this House with "the work that has been done by the Canadian Association for the Prevention of Tuberculosis; in doing that, I do not wish to conceal the fact that my desire is to influence this government to make a larger grant to that association. I have been interested in and connected with the work of the association for several years, and it has been deemed to be due to this government, which has made an annual grant to the association for some years past, and due to this parliament that a fairly full account should be given of the manner in which the association has expended that money. The Canadian Association for the Prevention of Tuberculosis was founded in 1899 at the instance of Lord Minto, then Governor General of Canada. In the early days of the association, its income was very small, and it could only attempt small things. In 1902 this government made a grant to the association of $1,000. In the following year the association engaged as its secretary the Rev. Dr. Moore, a Presbyterian minister who was greatly interested in the subject, a man of culture, tact and good judgment. Dr. Moore has continued in the service of the association as its secretary, and perhaps to no one person is due more than to him the success which has attended its efforts. For some time after Dr. Moore was engaged as secretary, the greater part of the work of the association was dope by and through him. His time was employed in part in the circulation of literature, which was mailed from the central office in Ottawa, and in part in delivering lectures throughout the Dominion. I do not think the association could have found any man within or without the medical profession whose lectures would have attracted more attention, aroused greater interest, provoked more inquiries or disseminated more information than the lectures given by this gentleman. I know this from reports which I have heard of his lectures and from having listened to one of his lectures myself. From those lectures much good has resulted.
In 1903 the Canadian government increased the grant of $1,000 to $2,000 and continued for some years after 1903 to give the increased sum per annum. In 1908

and 1909 the government was generous enough and wise enough to give the association an increased grant yearly of $5,000. These donations enabled the association to extend its work and the splendid results attained were soon apparent all over the land. In addition to the lectures delivered by Dr. Moore, and the circulation of literature, the association prepared articles and reports for the newspapers, and I desire to express the thanks of the association to the newspaper press of Canada for the liberal and prominent space they gave to these reports and articles. From the establishment of the association in 1899 to the present day, nine general annual meetings have been held, eight in Ottawa, which is the headquarters of the association, and the last one in Hamilton, Ontario. At each of these meetings addresses on the subject of tuberculosis, the best means of combatting it and preventing it, have been addressed by eminent medical men, most of them gentlemen who because of their special experience were peculiarly fitted to discuss the subject intelligently. Among the medical men who have addressed these annual gatherings have been Dr. Knopf of New York, Dr. Ravanel of Philadelphia, Dr. White of Pittsburg, Professor Adami of Montreal, the present president of the association, Drs. Richer and Laberge of Montreal, Dr. Sir James Grant and Dr. Bryce of Ottawa and Dr. Sheard of Toronto. The annual reports of the association have contained the addresses delivered by these eminent medical men together with a full report of the criticisms, notes and suggestions made by other medical men who were present at these gatherings. The annual general meetings of the association show clearly the awakened interest in this important subject throughout the Dominion for they have always been well attended by prominent medical and public spirited citizens from all over Canada. These annual reports have been mailed each year to persons who were known to take an interest in the subject and to great numbers of others who have written to the secretary requesting copies. Since 1899 when the association was established, fifty-five branch associations have been formed in different parts of Canada and there is no doubt at all but that these fifty-five associations were organized very largely through the influence of tile parent organization in whose behalf I speak to-night. Last winter Dr. Page of Quebec was instrumental in calling a public meeting which was attended by prominent citizens and as a result a local association was formed in the ancient capital. Since 1891 seven sanatoria have been erected in Canada, due largely to the interest awakened in the subject by the Canadian association for the prevention of tuberculosis. Free dispensaries have been
established in Winnipeg, Toronto, Hamilton, Montreal, Ottawa and Halifax. A great deal of literature has been distributed by the association and this literature has been written in plain English, which the lay people can understand. This literature has I believe taught the people who read it the best methods of stamping' out the disease, of preventing contagion and infection, and taking care of the unfortunate patients. Here are some samples of this literature:	Here is a little pamphlet
entitled ' Consumption-treatment at home, and rules for living,' this is an English publication written by H. Wassen Trowe, M.D.; here is another little pamphlet entitled ' Social and medical diseases by A. J. Richer, M.D., Montreal,' here is a paper written by Sir James Grant, upon our children ; here is a leaflet that has been widely circulated, entitled 1 How to prevent consumption '; another entitled ' Inspection of milk and meat '; another entitled ' Inspection of schools and school children '; another entitled ' consumption, its cause, treatment, and prevention.' Literature of this kind printed in the English and French languages has been circulated so persistently that including the literature now on hand it will amount to 7,000,000,000 pages. This literature has been systematically circulated and those employed in distributing it take the voters' lists of the municipalities as the mailing lists from which to make the distribution. So great has been the interest taken by the people of the country generally in^ this literature that in advance of the mailing many applications have been coming in from all over Canada asking the secretary to send literature. Many hundreds of letters have been received from all parts of the country expressing appreciation of this literature and the thanks of the recipients. The head office of the association in Ottawa has been a general information bureau; people in every province of the Dominion haye been constantly writing to the secretary for all kinds of instruction. Letters have come from the individual patient wanting to know how to regulate his diet and his habits of living; letters have come from friends, members of whose families have been afflicted, and letters have come from communities who contemplate the building of sanatoria asking for plans and estimated cost and such details. All of these letters have been promptly and carefully replied to. Lecturers of the association have lectured not only at public meetings specially called for the purpose, but at medical associations, normal schools, colleges, the senior departments of public schools, teachers associations, farmers gatherings and all kinds of public assemblies. The lecturer of the association at these gatherings has been a most welcome guest and has been most carefully listened to. Dr.

Valin, professor of Hygiene of Laval university is now engaged by the association to lecture on tuberculosis in the French tongue throughout the province of Quebec.
In 1908, our association was fortunate in securing the services of Dr. George D. Porter. Dr. Porter was engaged by the association as associate secretary and travelling lecturer. The experiences of Dr. Porter's own life have peculiarly fitted him for the work in which he is now engaged. He is not only an enthusiast, but an expert, and not only an expert, but an enthusiast- the right man in the right place.
Hear, hear.
