Now, I have been connected with the work of this association only for the last two or three years. I feel that some mention ought to be made and some credit given to the persons who have borne the brunt of the work of the association, those *who formed the organization and have since helped in carrying on the work. I realize that, with my partial knowledge of the work, should I attempt to mention the names of those who are most entitled to credit in the early times of the association when it often met with discouragements- for those were days when the public interest was not manifested in the subject as it is to-day-I should omit some names perhaps as'well worthy of our thanks as those whom I shall mention. Yet I desire to name some to whom the thanks of this whole Dominion are due for the time and the talent and energy that they have devoted to the work of the association. I l ave already stated that the association was instituted at the suggestion of the Earl of Minto. To him is due, therefore, a very large measure of credit for what has been accomplished. His Excellency Earl Grey, our present Governor General, has been and is the honorary president of the association. He has not been a mere figurehead, but has taken an active, intelligent and helpful interest in the work. He has been personally present at some of the annual meetings, has delivered addresses and has shown his sympathy in many ways, has also given many useful hints that have been of real help to the association. The association has had no better, warmer, or more consistent friend than Hon. Mr. Fisher, the Minister of Agriculture. His time has been so fully taken up with other things that it has not been possible for him to be present at all the meetings of the association, yet he has kept himself informed of what is doing, has kept constantly in touch with the work and has given the association valuable advice and information and has been indeed a real friend. 1 may mention also Mr. Courtney, who was treasurer of the association and is now honorary treasurer. He laboured faithfully and well in the interests of the association. I would recall also the name of Senator Edwards, one of the earlier presidents of the association. I am not well acquainted with the work which Senator Edwards did, because he has not, since I became connected with the association, taken an active part, as I understand he did in the early days. The association has had no more ardent, practical, consistent friend than Mr. Geo. H. Perley, M.P., the mover of this resolution. I will also mention the names of Sir
James Grant, of Dr. Small, of Mr. Manuel, of Dr. Montizambert and of Dr. Rutherford. All these gentlemen have aided very materially to bring about the success that has attended the efforts of the association. These men. you will observe, are all of the city of Ottawa, the head office of the association is in Ottawa; it is then a matter of necessity that the persons who take a prominent part and bear the brunt of the routine work are men resident of the city. But I would call your attention to this further fact, that Drs. Daniel, Black and Schaffner, and Mr. Barker, members of this House of Commons, are on the executive of the association; and while they have not attended all the meetings they have attended many of the executive meetings of the association. The association had the benefit of their knowledge, the benefit of their suggestions, and they have been exceedingly helpful. Then I point out that prominent medical men, and prominent public spirited men outside the profession, from one end of Canada to the other, have been very helpful indeed to the work of the association, helpful _ by their correspondence and the suggestions they have made by correspondence, and by attending the annual meetings, and exceedingly helpful to the association by carrying on field work in the localities in which they respectively live. I want to say that the work of the association has not been a local work, it has been a work extending from ocean to ocean, a work extending from the United States border line away to the far north, farther north than the white man has yet chosen permanently to reside.
It has been a work carried on in both French and English, and many lectures have been delivered in both French and English. The literature of the society has been printed in both languages. The aim, the object of the association has been to enlighten the ignorant and to help the poor. When I say to enlighten the ignorant, I mean to enlighten those who have been ignorant of the great facts concerning this dread disease. I would say that the aim of the association has been to help the poor. The association has helped the rich as well as the poor, but in this as in every other case those most needing help have been the poor who, because of their poverty have been unable to help themselves.
The question may well be asked, the question has been asked: Why has not the work of the association been carried _ on by private subscription? Sir, it is just as easy to answer that question as it is to ask it. It was, I think, well answered by the hon. member for Argenteuil who moved the resolution, when he said that the aim of the central organization is to promote the establishment of branch associations. The moment you establish a branch as-

sociation you establish a centre to which of necessity must be contributed all the funds that can b*e gathered in that locality for carrying on the local work. The bon. member for Argenteuil has given an instance of that as relating to the work in the city of Ottawa, where local public spirited men have contributed liberally and generously to the construction and maintenance of a hospital in the city, and to other work carried on within the city. It is not possible for every local association to build a hospital or sanatorium, but in the smaller local communities, in the smaller villages and towns, in rural centres where local associations are formed, it will be their duty to see that every consumptive patient within their territory is practically taken care of in their own homes where they may be provided with proper medical care, with proper nursing, with proper food, where they lack either means or intelligence to obtain that food for themselves. It will be the work of the local associations in such places to see that sputum cups are provided, and that every possible means is taken by proper sanitary regulations in order that there may not be contagion and infection carrying the disease to others as well as to those already affected.
Sir, it has been pointed out that this government has expended over a million and a half dollars in the last five years in preventing and stamping out disease in domestic animals. No one has found fault with that, no one will. It has been a very important work, properly and well carried out. But, Sir, if it is a praiseworthy work to expend a million and a half in five years to cure diseases of horses, cattle, sheep and swine that are in the barnyards, it is at least as important and much more important to spend large sums for the cure of men, women and children who are in the dwelling houses. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and I want to say to this government, that every single dollar that has been given by the government to the association has been economically, wisely and carefully spent. It has surprised me to see how exceedingly careful the expenditure of every single dollar was weighed and considered before the expenditure was ventured upon.
It may be said that if this association depends, as I admit that it does depend, almost entirely, one might say entirely, upon the government for its income-it may be said that it is really a government undertaking, and some may say, as I have heard some say around me to-night, that if the government provides the whole amount, the government might as well take over the work. But I wish to say that even though we admit that it is really and substantially the work of the government, yet I say that the work is being better carried Mr. MILLER.
on, more economically carried on, than it could possibly be carried on by any department of the government. Why? Because this work being carried on by a private association receives the gratuitous assistance, the gratuitous aid of clever, earnest and zealous men, aid which the government could not obtain gratuitously, and that is a very important consideration.
Further, let me say that gentlemen interested in the association recently approached the railways of the country and asked them to provide free passes for carrying to and fro the lecturers of the association; and I want to convey the thanks of the association to the railway companies for their generosity. The Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk railway, the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Intercolonial railway have cheerfully and readily given free passes to the lecturers of the association. This effects a considerable saving that would not have been effected, and would not have been asked, and if asked would not have been granted, had the government been carrying on the work.
Now, Sir, in conclusion let me read to you this resolution recently passed at an executive meeting of the association. The resolution passed within the last week or ten days is as follows:
Ikat the association finds it quite impossible to carry on its work as it would like to no and teels that it ought to do, with its present small revenue. The association has endeavoured to send out over the whole Dominion, suitable literature, in the French language in the French districts, and in English throughout the remainder of the Dominion. And also to keep in the field continuously a medical lecturer, and other medical lecturers for portions of the year. The association has been much encouraged by the undoubted evidences of the splendid success of its work to date, and respectfully requests the parliament of Canada to largely increase this year the annual grant which they have been good enough to make to the association.
Now, Sir, in conclusion I have to thank the government on behalf of the association for their liberality, for their generosity in years that are past, and at the same time to ask the government, to ask parliament, to increase the grant this year from $5,000 to at least $10,000. The hon. member who placed this resolution on the Order Paper, in the last part of it, uses these words:
This House is of the opinion that parliament should now take more active steps to further lessen the great suffering and mortality caused by this disease.
I think, although I have no authority to speak for him, that the mover of the resolution and that the Canadian Association for the Prevention of Tuberculosis will accept it as carrying out of the meaning

in this resolution if the government will be liberal enough to grant the association, for the present year, the sum of $10,000

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) deserves the thanks of this House and of the people of Canada at large..
I trust this House will not share the opinion that parliament should take more determined steps to still further reduce the great sufferings; and the number of deaths caused by consumption. Yes, it is our duty to make the most strenuous efforts to reduce the rate of sickness and death caused by tuberculosis in our country. Canada loses 8,000 lives every year by that dreaded disease, while 40,000 persons are suffering with it in the various provinces of the Dominion. Allow me in view of these alarming figures to read an important page concerning the work that is being done in the state of Rhode Island to stay the progress of tuberculosis:
Despite its wealth, its strength and its prosperity, is the American nation in a position to throw absolutely away every year the , sum of $430,000,000?
This is the question which is put to the public by the Rhode Island Anti-Tuberculosis Association. According to secretary Wallace Hatch, the white plague means to the nation an annual loss of $430,000,000.
This loss of money and the still more deplorable loss of thousands of lives each year will be stopped as soon as the anti-tuberculosis associations which are at work in the whole extent of this country have succeeded in teaching the people at large the essential facts relating to the cause, the treatment and the prevention of this terrible disease.
The brightest future is confronting the workers in Rhode Island. They announce a very effective work already begun and to be pursued. The state board of health and those of the leading cities are doing inestimable service to the cause. Education boards are opening schools of instruction. Hygienic rules are printed dn the text books and doctors are permitted to address the pupils in schools.
Manufacturers on the other hand are contributing to the great popular movement of educating the masses by including in the pay envelopes printed rules on hygiene, by posting up useful informations in their shops and by recommending to their sick employees to report to local or nearby associations. Lectures are also delivered to the workingmen.
Ministers of the church lend their influential and benevolent support to the movement in their respective pulpits.
Many more private and public organizations do their utmost to help the authorities.
Every year this great regenerating movement in the United States which ds intended to snatch the white race from this plague that strikes at the country's vitals and open up every year iso many thousands of graves for youthful victims is making immense progress. The future of the nation is at stake. The work will only stop when the last man, the last woman, the last child in the country
will have intimately identified himself with it, and when the last track of tuberculosis has for ever vanished from the American soil.
We must for the sake of humanitarian-ism and in the interest of the people of Canada follow that wise advice and we will be able thereby to maintain our nation to the fore among the other nations of the world We join in the generous work accomplished by our elder brothers. Our doctors attended the anti-tuberculosis congress held at Washington in September, 1908. Medical men and the public at large in the city of Montreal are not indifferent to modern progress, and they endeavour to battle against the fearful foe. I read the following lines in the "Union Medicate du Canada" of December 1, 1909:
On November 29, 1902, a number of gentlemen prominent in the world of finance, industry and commerce, as well as in the professions, informed on the one hand with the means employed in the various countries for the prevention of tuberculosis and on the other, feeling justly alarmed at the ravages of the disease in our city, founded in a public meeting held under the patronage or liis Excellency the Governor General of Canada an association for the protection of the people against consumption. . .
Then the "Union Medicate" shows the happy results which crowned the efforts of those real philanthropists. Quebec city has also organized an anti-tuberculosis association, but this government must not remain idle. Here is what Dr. Rousseau said at the medical congress held at Three Rivers:
The government cannot remain indifferent in presence of the greatest social evil which exists. We do not expect them to do all that is to be done but we do expect them to do their share of educating work. Their imperative duty consists in spreading information and helping every anti-tuberculosis movement.
The rector of Laval University at Quebec, wishing to help in fighting the awful disease, invited Dr. Rousseau, in March, 1909, to deliver a lecture at the University on the nature of tuberculosis and the conditions in which it will develop. Allow me to read the last page of his lecture:
You cannot think nowadays of insolating the consumptive; of tearing him violently away from his surroundings before his sad death.
But let assistance be tendered them; let some guidance, some help be extended to them in the fulfilment of their arduous duties towards their kindred and towards society: either in a sanatorium, in a hospital or in their own homes, properly isolated, let them find conditions of comfort and safety which are not generally available to such patients. That iis what we are in a position to do and what we should do; there lies the way out, provided generous contributions are forthcoming.

But we prefer dickering, dilly-dallying in the hope perhaps, a vain hope for the time being at any rate, that some great cure, some anti-tuberculosis serum will be discovered, though there is not the least foreboding of -such a discovery.
Now, when there are available to us efficient means of protection, it is unfair and unwise on our part to neglect them and be content with beseaching the medical profession to effect some wonderful discovery for our protection. Thus are we courting sad disappointment. Wealth, indeed, is more frequently met with than genius.
The government of the province of Quebec has appointed a royal commission to look into the means of preventing the spread of tuberculosis. I anticipate satisfactory results from the findings of that commission. However, if we are truly -anxious of wiping out all traces of tuberculosis from our Canadian soil, we should close our doors to tuberculous immigrants. To attain that great object, to meet the wishes laid down in the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from Argentueil, we should adopt better methods of inspection as regards immigrants. Men in good standing attach great importance to the medical examination as now effected at the shipping port. What reliance should we put in such inspection?
In the month of August, 1906, inspector B. Smith, of the Ontario charitable institutions (Report for 1908, page 16) noticed on a steamer a poor tuberculous immigrant who could hardly walk. Of course, such an immigrant, on the verge of death, could not be admitted. He was deported by the authorities and died on reaching Glasgow. If the steamship company's medical officer had thought of casting an eye on that poor man, he would not have permitted him to board the ship. Disease was fast carrying away that immigrant, heartbroken and disappointed as he was. The whole system is a downright mockery. I have evidence from the best sources to uphold me in this. According to Doctor D. Page, immigrants at the shipping ports in Europe are subjected to a superficial examination only. According to Dr. Bryce, the inspection effected at the shipping ports does not differ from the ordinary routine of the steamship companies.
The Immigration Act provides that all persons suffering from contagious or infectious diseases shall be excluded. Consumption of the lungs which represents the last phases of tuberculosis, should certainly he included among the diseases of a contagious and infectious character. The laws of the United States specially mention tuberculosis, and rightly so. Now on May
10.	1909, the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson), requested that the Minister of the Interior should make provision for the exclusion of tuberculous immigrants. The hon. minister's answer was rather startling: Mr. PAQTJET.
' We all admit, he said, the advisability of excluding those who are suffering from tuberculosis, but its diagnosis is a difficult matter at its various stages, and we would bo imposing on the department a task which they could not fulfil in a satisfactory manner.' I deplore this woeful expression of opinion, this extraordinary stand on the part of the minister.
As regards the greater number of immigrants sent to Canada by charitable associations, the trade carried on, the air breathed in the factories, the overcrowding in tenements, poor ventilation, scarcity of light and suitable food are so many factors concerning which the authorities should exert the closest supervision. The proportion of people affected or dying from tuberculosis in British cities, whence thousands of immigrants come to Canada, is verj high. Such immigrants should be submitted to a very searching examination of the respiratory organs.
In 1906, at the meetings of the anti-tuberculosis association, Dr. Page submitted an interesting paper on tuberculosis from the standpoint of immigration. He showed how dangerous was the situation and tried to indicate a remedy. Indeed the members of the association at once appointed a committee to interview the hon. Minister of the Interior. The latter promised to take the most energetic steps towards excluding tuberculous people. Notwithstanding which, on May 10, 1909, the hon. minister refused to include tuberculosis in the list of diseases entailing exclusion.
Tuberculous immigrants are coming in. Dr. Page, in the course of the civil service investigation spoke as follows: ' A certain number of tuberculous immigrants may escape our attention. The disease is difficult to diagnose at its inception, and we have not enough time at our disposal to make the required examination Such a startling statement points to the absolute insufficiency of our system of medical inspection. In the crusade we are waging against this most disastrous disease, it is to the government we must appeal for guidance and help.
The hon. Minister of the Interior taking heed of the progress of scientific discovery, should lay down as a rule the exclusion of tuberculous immigrants. He should increase the number of our medical inspectors at all large ports. He should promptly adopt a system whereby these medical men would be in a position to carry on careful examinations with the object of detecting any incipient case of tuberculosis. I am aware that the diagnosis of that disease is not always an easy matter. Certain forms evolve insidiously, and little by little leave an impress on the organism. However, tuberculous people cannot readily escape detection by competent physicians, provided

the latter have enough time allowed them to permit a thorough investigation. In March, 1908, Dr. Bryce seems to think that the difficulties in the way of diagnosing cases of tuberculosis were sufficient to excuse the introduction of tuberculous immigrants into Canada. He even went so far as to quote high medical authorities with a view to proving that such diagnosis in a great many cases can be obtained only at an advanced stage of the disease. The stand taken by Dr. Brice seems to me most regrettable as regards the selection of immigrants. According to the most renowned clinicians, the diagnosis of incipient tuberculosis can be obtained by a series of clinical symptoms and phenomena following the injection of tuberculine. At the very outset, that is in the stage of primary development of the tubercles, the physician who undertsands auscultation is in a position to diagnose a case of tuberculosis. Through the use of the microscope and a knowledge of bacteriology, and by means of the X rays, cases of that disease may be diagnosed at the outset. The possibility of detecting incipient cases of tuberculosis imparts great practical interest to the examination of immigrants. We are sadly at fault when admitting tuberculous immigrants into Canada. Not only is there danger of contaminating the present generation of Canadians, but also of transmitting this tuberculous taint to future generations.
An incomplete, -insufficient medical examination is apt to give the worst results. Tuberculous immigrants begin by contaminating some of their fellow-travellers on board ship. Then they contaminate people with whom they live in Canada, and imperil the health and existence of the whole community. Previous to 1904 there existed no systematic inspection of immigrants. The government then recognized the necessity of medical intervention with a view to ascertaining what immigrants were possessed of sufficient brains to understand the working of our institutions and live in harmony with our people, while helping on our national progress. That was a step in advance ; however, legislation is still very imperfect. If we really have at heart our country's welfare, we are bound to improve our methods of inspection, in such a way as to exclude all tuberculous immigrants.

Mr. Speaker, I would not address the House at this late hour were it not that by remaining silent I might be misunderstood as either opposed to the resolution or not sufficiently interested in one of the most important subjects that can at any time engage the attention of the Canadian parliament. The knowledge that medical men have of the ravages of this disease and the possibility of curing hundreds of thousands of cases, in addition to relieving the
sufferings of a verv large number, lengthening their lives and minimizing the danger r f their presence amongst others, is such that no medical man can be indifferent to this very important question. There is equally good work open for us to do, whether it is by education, by hygiene, by prophylaxis, which is preventing, or by providing better food for the people. It is sufficient to engage the philanthropic attention of the best minds, not only of the medical profession to-day, but of any class of people in the community. It is said: How can we, the Canadian parliament, assist in this good work? It is claimed by some that it is not within our province to assist this work. This association aims purely at the dissemination of information. When has parliament disclaimed its right to give assistance in disseminating knowledge? Never. Since I came into the Canadian parliament or so far as I am aware before that time, it has never been claimed that it was unconstitutional or improper for this parliament to aid in the dissemination of information. We give money for the dissemination of information in a great many lines outside of that which claims our attention to-night. Many years ago we accented the principle and voted yearly $2,000 for the purpose of publishing a health magazine, or a bureau of statistics and health for the purpose of dealing with sanitary subjects. That was kept up for many years under Dr. Playter, and I do not think any one complained at the giving of that amount of money nor was it considered that there was not an ample return to the country for its expenditure. I claim that parliament can spend monev for any purpose it likes, there was no interference with our right either in the British North America Act or any other Act. We can subsidize anything we desire, we can give money for any purpose we wish. We subsidize the building of railways by money grants, we give money to steamships, we vote money to employ lecturers to instruct the farmers with reference to- diseases of plants, grain, fruit and all vegetable diseases. No one objects to this nor does any one say it is wrong. We give aid to lectures to the farmers with regard to the diseases of animals, and why can we not as well vote money to disseminate information with regard to what is above all these others in importance, the health of our people. If we vote monev for these purposes in relation to plants and animals, whv can we not do it in the interest of the great human family? It is said that from 8,000 to 10,000 die annually of this disease in Canada. If we can do anything to lessen that number, surely a donation of money is not out of place. We mav lessen the death rate by disseminating knowledge, teaching the peo-

pie how to prevent and combat that disease. It you educate people so that they will understand how to prevent consumption, how to care for themselves by better hygienic surroundings when affected by it, how to isolate themselves, you will go a long way towards lessening the death rate from consumption. But we can go further and educate the people to care for themselves from a sanitary and dietetic point of view, teaching them the value of fresh air and of favourable surroundings. To mv mind if we gave instead of $4,000 or $5,000, a couple of hundred thousand, not one word of complaint would be heard in the country. But we must do more than educate, we must prevent it if possible. It has been said that the Indian cannot bear civilization, he dies off when you civilize him. What is meant by civilization? Taking him out of the wigwam, removing him from his outdoor life, and placing him in a close sealed house. The result is that consumption carries off thousands of Indians, and if the Indians were compelled to live in the same kind of lath and plaster house that the white man lives in it would be only a few years until they would be wiped out. Why is it so few Indians die when living a nomadic life? Because the fresh air, by vitalizing the blood, prevents the development of the bacilli favourable to tuberculosis in the human economy.
We must check consumption by supplying pure food. We must go beyond the disease among human beings and secure immunity from the disease in animals as well. In a report of the United States Department of Agriculture for 1905, I find some statistics bearing on this which are of importance to us. We eat a great deal of beef and pork in this country. The United States Department of Agriculture state that out of 25,000,000 hogs slaughtered in one year in the United States, 217,000 were affected with tuberculosis. Out of 6,000,000 cattle 11,000 were affected with tuberculosis but out of 8,000,000 sheep only 27 were so affected. That is only one sheep in every 295,550 was affected with tuberculosis whilst amongst the cattle there were 555 in every 291,000 and amongst the hogs there were 2,393 affected with tuberculosis in every 291,000. Ought not this to teach us a very important lesson- that we are eating very much of that kind of meat which has in it the greatest elements of danger to the human family, and that of the three kinds of meat, mutton and lamb are what we should prefer if we desire to avoid that danger. We must attack this disease not only by education, but by building up a stronger and more vital physical constitution in the people, because the stronger the constitution the less liable it will be to the inroads of the disease. This is the reason for the im-

portance of supplying the human family with good food, whether it is butter, meat, cheese or milk, in all of which the tuberculosis bacillus is found. The fact that thousands of infants are fed on milk which is largely tuberculous means that if these children grow up to manhood and womanhood they will have less vigorous constitutions to resist the disease than those who have been fed on pure food. How important it is, therefore, that we should attack tuberculosis in the dairies and in the herds of cattle and swine as well as in the human economy. In all of these directions we should spend money freely. A few years ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture if he had made any calculation of how long it would take to eradicate tuberculosis from the herds of our country. I do not remember what his answer was, but one who knew whereof he spoke said that we could eradicate it in a few years if we were willing to pay enough money to do the work. How valuable this would be to the many thousands of young children who live largely or chiefly on milk. This subject is too important to be set aside by any quibbles about our constitutional rights under the British North America Act. That Act does not stand in the way of our doing our duty in this matter. We build marine hospitals which will harbour tuberculosis patients as well as others. We can grant money for technical education to the farmer and the horticulturist. Why can we not grant money to educate the men who look after the health of the human family? In mv judgment we can do it, and I hope the Minister 9f Agriculture will give the House an intimation to night that the government have reached the conclusion that there is a valuable work in this matter that can and should be done, and that towards that work they are prepared to give adequate assistance.

Mr. Speaker, let me first congratulate the proposer of this resolution not only on the manner in which he has presented a complex and important question to the House, but also on the untiring enthusiasm and industry which he has displayed for many years past in presenting the question to the public of Canada as well as to the House. I also wish to join with my hon. friend from Grey in saying a word of praise and congratulation "to the members of the Canadian Association for the Prevention of the Spread of Tuberculosis. The gentlemen who have been engaged in this work have been doing sometimes" a very discouraging and sometimes, as it appeared to be, a thankless *work. But they have persisted in their efforts, until at last I think they have been able to show a measure of success which calls for the recognition and gratitude of the people of the country. In speaking on this question, let me at once, in response

to the appeal of my hon. friend from Grey, say that I wish to support the resolution, and I hope the House will adopt it with unanimity so as to show to the people of the country that this House fully realizes the importance of and entirely sympathizes with every method that can possibly be adopted for stamping out this very dangerous malady. I am prepared to say that as no new step is asked of us by the present motion, I believe the government will be ready to recognize the appeal of the House and ask for further aid for the Canadian association. In doing this we are adopting no new plan or taking no new step which might bring us into conflict with the constitution or with the provincial authorities. I am glad that on this occasion the debate has taken that course. I am glad that W'e are not asked, as we were on a former occasion, to do something that we could not see our way to doing. My hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) quoted some remarks of mine made five years ago. Well, I have no objection to my remarks being quoted, although five years have passed, but I would like to point out to my hon. friend that I was then discussing a totally different proposition. We were then being asked to grant aid for the establishment of sanatoria in Canada-to do something which by the British North America Act is in definite words relegated to the provincial authorities. I do not wish to discuss to any great extent the question of the British North America Act, but I must confess that I am not as prepared to trespass upon the special purview of the provincial authorities as my hon. friend from Argen-teuil seems to think we ought to be. I do not consider that the illustration which he gave of the man in 'the burning house offending against a technical ordinance was a good one, because the question of the powers relegated by the British North America Act to the provincial authorities and to this parliament respectively is in no sense technical.
When that Act was drawn up those things which were more local in their character were placed under the control of the provinces and those things which were of a more general nature were entrusted to this parliament. I have no hesitation in believing that the framers of that legislation, after careful consideration and study, have given good reason for the disposition of the items in that Act. Under these circumstances I hesitate to undertake to overstep the bounds of the authority of this parliament and to enter the provincial sphere. The question of education and the question of the action of my own department has been cited here to-night, but I would point out to my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) that when the Agricultural Department undertakes to deal with agricultural subjects it is not dealing with what is technically called edhcation. Education as I understand it in the terms of the British North America Act, is the education of the youth of the country, and not the giving of information to the grown people who are engaged in our various industries, agriculture among the number. The department over which I have the honour for the moment to preside has not in any way undertaken the education of the young people of the country by means of schools or colleges. What it has done is to conduct experiments in agriculture and to place the results of these experiments before the people for their benefit. There is a well-defined difference between that sort of work and the education of the youth. I would say, further, that the work of the Department of Agriculture is very similar to the work of the association for the prevention of tuberculosis, and I,am, therefore, quite at one with the movement to have this government grant any reasonable request for circulating information calculated to check the spread of disease. I am glad to know that the provinces have fully recognized their responsibility in regard to hospitals or sanataria. Several of the provinces have already established these hospitals and my friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) has sent me photographs of a very beautiful and I am sure complete and well equipped sanatorium at Ninette, in Manitoba. I know that the province of British Columdia has established a sana-tarium and I think the province of Nova Scotia has done something of a similar character. My hon. friend from LTslet (Mr. Paquette) told us that the government of the province of Quebec has not yet established a sanatorium, but that it has appointed a commission to investigate tuberculosis and to furnish information as to how that province may best deal with this dread disease. The provinces, therefore, are meeting their responsibilities in this respect and I do not think it would be at all advisable for this parliament to overlap the work they are doing or to try to duplicate it. Let me say a word with regard to what we are doing in reference to the health of animals. Some hon. gentlemen have drawn the conclusion that we are spending much more money on the health of animals than we are for the health of the human being, but I would like to say here at once that every cent spent in Canada for the health of animals is really spent for the health of the human being. We are looking after the animals because we want to ensure that the human being may be certain that the meat he eats, the milk he drinks and the products of the animal which he consumes shall be wholesome. Of course, the regulations in regard to the treatment of animals for disease are very much more simple than they could

possibly be in the case of the human being, because, in the public interest, we can slaughter diseased animals where that becomes necessary. Of the money expended in the last few years in connection with the health of animals, about $700,000 has been paid as compensation for animals slaughtered, and that for the purpose of seeing that disease is not spread which is inimical to the human being. It is true that the Department of Agriculture deals with quarantine, but when you compare the money spent for the health of animals with the money spent for the protection of the health of the human being, you must eliminate from the former the large sums which are paid as compensation for the animals killed. Even in that view I reiterate that the money spent in connection with the health of animals is spent for the benefit of the health of the people of the country and not' primarily or essentially for the protection of other animals against disease. Let me say that I do not believe there is any other country which can to-day present such a clean bill of health for its domestic animals as Canada can. In this connection I feel it my duty to take up the cudgels in defence of the Canadian cow. There is a tendency abroad to lay pretty nearly all the tuberculosis in the country to tubercular milk. Well, I have made a good deal of investigation and I have studied the question carefully, and from the information I have been able to get I am prepared to say that not 10 per cent of the tuberculosis in Canada can in any way be traced to the consumption of tubercular milk. There is the tuberculin test which can be applied to animals and that will test the presence of tuberculosis in any form in any part of the animal, but we have shown conclusively from experiments that the milk from a tuberculous animal in numberless instances contains no active germ Of tuberculosis which could possibly communicate tuberculosis to any human being who drinks it. There is this unfortunate fact, however, in connection with the tuberculin test, and it is the chief weakness of the test, that while the test almost absolutely shows whether there is any tubercle in the animal it does not show where the tubercle is nor the extent of the tubercle, and especially it does not show whether the tubercle in the animal can affect the purity of the milk or on the other hand the presence of disease germs in it.
Under these circumstances, while the tuberculin test does place any animal that reacts to it under suspicion, and though that animal may have in its udder and in its milk the germs of tuberculosis which may infect the person consuming that milk, the fact that the animal reacts to the tuberculin test is absolutely no proof whatever that its milk will be dangerous to a person I Mr. FISHER.
drinking it. Personally, I would not drink the milk of any animal that reacted to the test because I would wish to spend my money rather upon safeguarding myself than in the purchase of cheaper milk that was not so safeguarded. At the same time it would . be the height of folly, and I think it is to-day a mistake for people to believe or expect that the animals should be slaughtered simply because they have reacted to the tuberculin test. I state this with a full sense of my responsibility in so doing. I say it because I have studied the question for many years and because I have had experience of the disease in my own barns and my own herds, and I have seen the effect of it in other herds. Also, I have been in charge for thirteen years of the experiments of the scientific veterinaries who have examined into this question continuously ever since I entered office as minister. I wish to say further that, at present, we are trying to find some method, some sensible, practical method, not too extreme, not unnecessarily severe on the owners of stock, by which we can deal with tuberculosis among cattle, among cows especially.

Does not the minister think he should attach more importance to the danger of drinking milk that may be infected with tuberculosis? What does he make of the experiments of Senator Edwards? Senator Edwards took calves from cows affected with tuberculosis and, from the first, gave them pure milk from other cows, and, as I vmderstand the matter in discussing it with the senator, not in one case did he find the tuberculosis present in the young animal. Is it not likely that milk is one of the means by which the disease is transferred from the dam?

I think the hon. member has misunderstood me. I said that personally I would not drink the milk of any animal that reacted to the tuberculin test. That animal is under suspicion. But I know, from abundant experiments, that the milk of a great many animals that react to the tuberculin test does not contain the germs of tuberculosis. If the milk does contain the germs of tuberculosis, of course it is-dangerous; but the fact that a cow reacts to the tuberculin test is absolutely no proof that her milk will contain tuberculosis germs. Do not let me be misunderstood. I do not wish people to cease trying to remove tuberculosis from the cows of the country. I think that every means ought to be taken to accomplish that object, so-long as we step on sure ground. But to undertake the slaughter of innumerable animals without being perfectly sure that their slaughter is necessary for the health of human beings would be folly and a wrongful waste of a great asset of the people of Canada.

I was going to say, when I was interrupted, that at a meeting of the North American Veterinary Association last summer, Dr. Rutherford, the chief veterinary officer of my department was present, and he secured the appointment of a joint committee of American and Canadian veterinary surgeons, which committee is to meet, I think, this week in Buffalo for the purpose of trying to elaborate a practical, sane treatment of cows for the purpose 'of minimizing tuberculosis in our herds. I hope and believe that a scheme will be elaborated by that body of men, probably the best experts on that question to be found anywhere, and that it will be able to present shortly to the department at Washington and to my own department a scheme for practical steps to further reduce tuberculosis.
Now, I began a few minutes ago by saying our herds were healthy, that we have not a very large percentage of cattle or swine in Canada affected by tuberculosis, and hardly any sheep so affected. We have had, for some years past, a very strict system of inspection of all the meat packing establishments in Canada which are engaged in the export trade. Our veterinary surgeons have carefully examined every animals carcass taken into these establishments, and the percentage of rejections and condemnations for tuberculosis is so small as to justify absolutely what I have said. I have not before me the exact figures, but my recollection is that in the case of cattle the rejections are less than two per cent, and in the case of hogs less than five per cent. The animals slaughtered in these establishments come in from all over the country, without any inspection before they arrive, and without any selection, and yet [DOT]only a few of them are condemned for tuberculosis. Every carcass in the slightest degree affected by tuberculosis is condemned. Under these circumstances, I think I am justified in saying that the animals of Canada are exceptionally healthy and that the danger of communicating tuberculosis through food is not great. I have further the opinion of doctors and others who have discussed it with me that not ten per cent of tuberculosis is contracted through drinking any milk in Canada.
Now, let me say one or two things in regard to the requests made of us. I think it was my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) who spoke of the good we could do in the way of registration and notification. That is a matter, I think, purely local and municipal, and we can hardly entertain it *cr deal with it. I am glad that in this debate there has been no suggestion, as there was in former debates on the subject, that
we should undertake to build or aid the building of sanatoria. It is true that years ago when this question came up I objected to our undertaking the work, and I am glad that the whole tone of the debate to-day has justified that stand. The whole debate to-day shows that the matter is now regarded as one coming within the domain of provincial authority.
I desire to pay a tribute to the high order of this debate. The medical gentlemen have given us a great deal of very valuable information, information which I think ought to be placed before the public. I do not think the association can do any better work than to distribute all over Canada copies of the ' Hansard ' containing this debate. My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) interested me a great deal with the information he gave us as to what is being done in Germany. I will say this for the continental nations of Europe, that in dealing with the welfare of their people they are very thorough, they go to the root of things, and do not hesitate to pass rules and regulations which we would consider somewhat drastic, and perhaps which western peoples would not like to submit to. I believe this association has done a great deal in stirring up the people to the necessity of vigorous effort in combatting the disease of tuberculosis. I agree with the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Miller) that it is better that this work should be done by an association of citizens rather than by a department of the government. I cordially admit what the hon. member for Grey has said, that the association has spent their money wisely, carefully and economically. I congratulate the members of the association on their administration of the money that has been entrusted to them by parliament, and I have no doubt they will expend with equal wisdom and economy any further funds that may be granted them.
There is another point I would suggest, although it is a matter coming under the domain of the provincial authorities, and that is the problem of dealing with tuberculosis in public schools. That is a very serious problem indeed. It is certainly a hard thing to say that tubercular children must be excluded from the public schools. That cannot be done in any community without proper provision being made to secure to such children just as good an education outside the school as they could obtain within it. At the same time, it must be recognized that their presence is a menace to the health of other children, and as I say, it is one of the most painful problems that confronts us in connection with this disease. I believe, however, that in the erection and enlargement of our public schools, if more attention were paid to ventilation, more cubic air space were provided, as we know that plenty of fresh air

is extremely essential to the health of children, a great deal of danger would be removed, at any rate the danger would be minimized and, the general health of the pupils would be improved. Ill ventilation, over crowding, shutting out of the school room the cool fresh air of Canada, which is one of the best heritages we have, all these things contribute to the spread of tuberculosis among children.
Now if the House will bear with me, I would like to relate an experiment which we have been conducting with cattle, and it affords a lesson which might be of use to human beings. About four years ago the herd of cattle on the Nappan experimental farm contracted tuberculosis. It spread very rapidly through the barns, and in a few months practically all the animals were affected with tuberculosis. Dr. Rutherford wished very much to try an experiment with regard to the outdoor treatment of the animals. We brought the herd up here, and established them across the river in an isolated place nearby, where we kept them out of doors altogether for four years. Every animal was diseased when it came here. We added to the herd some other healthy animals, but no one of the healthy animals contracted the disease. Of the calves that were born to the diseased animals, born out of doors in healthy surroundings, and fed on their mothers' milk, not one was diseased. They are to-day healthy animals. I have no doubt whatever that the spread of tuberculosis amongst the dairy herds of this country is almost entirely due to the confinement in which these herds are kept, and that better ventilation of stables, byres more cleanly kept, with more sunshine and more light, would contribute more than anything else to the eradication of the disease from the herds. Of course these conditions are equally necessary, if not more necessary, to human beings. They are necessary in public buildings, they are necessary in private buildings, in schools perhaps first of all, and in all public buildings belonging to the government. One hon. gentleman spoke about what'we should do in regard to our public service. I sympathize with that view. The Civil Service Commission created a couple of years ago had that very question under consideration and no doubt in the near future an improvement may be made^ in that matter as regards the Civil Service. I will close by saying that I hope the House will pass this resolution unanimously. I can assure the House that the government is quite disposed to do all it can within its sphere in order to strengthen this campaign against tuberculosis.

As no one else wishes to sneak, I may sav that I appreciate highly the way in which this resolution has been received. I need hardly say I had no Mr. FISHER.
intention of treating the British North America Act with disrespect, or lightly, in any way; certainly I desire to live up to it as much as any other member of this House. I was only arguing that _ what we wished to have done would not in any *way interfere with it, either technically or otherwise. With regard to sanatoria, and the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture five years ago, I simply call attention to the fact that the resolution of five years ago made no mention of sanatoria, it was merely an academic resolution.
But the debate did.

It was an academic resolution, but I think that certain hon. gentlemen mentioned the building of a sanatorium. I quite acknowledge that under the British North America Act it would not be wise for this government, at the present time, at all events, to take any steps in that direction. I do not ask for it. I am very glad that the government has accepted this resolution and I simply conclude with the hope, after the kind words the Minister of Agriculture has spoken on this subject, that we mav expect in the supplementary, estimates a reasonable increase in the grant for this important work.
